coreStoryFacts.text: That's where Bitcoin works best as a hedge against inflation.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
One 2023 study, bluntly titled "Bitcoin Does Not Hedge Inflation," suggests that Bitcoin tends to fall during inflation scares.
That argues for holding other assets that will hold up against inflation, such as gold, index funds, and real estate, as well as some Bitcoin.

After all, even if it doesn't have the same history as gold, it's easy to see that Bitcoin's value isn't about to be inflated away anytime soon, whether or not it keeps up with gas prices during a major war.
So it's difficult to say that the coin is a good inflation hedge without adding some significant qualifications.
What's more, over the last five years, during which inflation has consistently run well above the Fed's 2% annual target, Bitcoin's price is up 32%.
Gold, the traditional inflation-resistant asset, is up by 129%, and the S&P 500 is up by 69%.
Consumer prices rose 22.8% from September 2021 to September 2026, per the BLS, so Bitcoin did beat inflation across five years.
Bitcoin is often proposed as a way to protect portfolios from inflation.

Bitcoin is mainly a bulwark against currency debasement, the dramatic erosion of a currency's purchasing power, most often caused by governments creating new money faster than the underlying economy grows.
It can succeed against debasement because no matter how much money gets printed, it's simply impossible to print more Bitcoin.
Still, that hedge actually working well is entirely unproven at this juncture.

With U.S. consumer prices up 3.7% through September 2026, many savers want to know whether Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) or gold is the better inflation hedge. This rise exceeds the Federal Reserve’s 2% target . Additionally, the core Consumer Price Index (CPI), which excludes the more volatile food and energy sectors, rose 0.3% in September alone.

Bitcoin is trading around $80,530, which is 36.1% lower than its all-time high. Over the past year, Bitcoin has decreased by 27.4%, and it’s down 4.4% in the last month. However, it has seen a rebound with a gain of 23.4% over the last three months.

Gold has also seen some dips. Tether Gold ( CRYPTO:XAUT ), a token that is backed by physical gold, is trading close to $3,990, down 27.5% from its peak on January 28, and it has decreased by 6.3% in the last month. So, which asset has performed better against inflation, and which one looks more promising as we head into 2027?

In a five-year comparison, gold has significantly outperformed Bitcoin. The price of spot gold increased by 126.1%, rising from $1,780 at the end of October 2021 to $4,024 on October 23, 2026. In contrast, Bitcoin only rose by 28% in the same timeframe, climbing from $62,990 on October 25, 2021.

From December 2021 to September 2026, the consumer price index increased by 19.8%. Both gold and Bitcoin outpaced inflation during this period, but gold performed much better. This trend continues over shorter timeframes as well; since December 2023, gold has gained 95.1%, while consumer prices have climbed just 8.9%.

However, the yearly results look different. From the end of October 2025, gold barely moved, losing 0.2%, while Bitcoin plummeted 27.4% even as prices rose 3.7%. In 2026 alone, Bitcoin has dropped about 8.0%, while gold is down about 7.6%, against a 3.2% increase in CPI since December 2025.

Gold encountered significant challenges during its most recent inflation tests. Consumer prices surged by 5.8% from January to December 2022, but gold fell by 15.7%, dropping from $1,936 at the end of March 2022 to $1,632 by the end of October 2022.
Gold has remained volatile in 2026, peaking at $5,279 on February 28, then falling to $4,012 by June 30 before bouncing back to $4,460 by August 31.

Bitcoin’s price movements are even more dramatic . For instance, it traded at $65,341 on July 26 and then soared to $84,385 by September 24, marking a staggering 29.1% increase in just two months. Over the past decade, Bitcoin has grown nearly 119-fold since its price was $678. While Bitcoin has protected purchasing power over the long term, its monthly fluctuations can be unreliable.

Global central banks are stockpiling gold at an accelerating pace, with some moving reserves out of the U.S. These official buyers generally hold gold for years, providing steady demand on a scale Bitcoin doesn’t have.

Additionally, the money supply continues to expand. As of August 2026, M2, which includes cash, checking deposits, savings, and money market funds, reached a five-year high of $23.3 trillion, up 5.7% year over year—within the normal 5% to 7% range.

Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan argues that Bitcoin’s primary advantage lies in its potential to protect investors from currency debasement, which occurs when increased currency supply reduces buying power. Yet, this value proposition hasn’t translated into a strong performance for Bitcoin in its one-year return.

Recent data suggests gold has been the stronger inflation hedge and appears more stable as we approach 2027. Over the past five years, gold has significantly outpaced inflation and remains a preferred choice, given buying activity from central banks.

While Bitcoin has also been a strong long-term hedge against inflation, it fell 27.4% in a year when prices rose 3.7%. Bitcoin tends to benefit holders who hold it for five years or more , despite sharp declines.

A few key price points could influence this assessment. If Bitcoin rebounds above $87,498, its December 31, 2025, price, it would effectively erase its 2026 losses—a rise of 8.7% from current levels. In contrast, gold trades just 0.3% above its June price of $4,012. A monthly close below that mark, while CPI remains near 3.7%, could diminish gold’s status as a solid hedge against inflation.

passages: Hot inflation could eventually help Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC), but the relationship between inflation and Bitcoin is a lot more complex than it seems.
Consumer prices rose by 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026, per the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), and Bitcoin fell about $1,000 on the hotter-than-expected Oct.
14 report, as hot inflation raises the odds of interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.
Still, there's an argument for why more inflation could be bullish for Bitcoin, so let's think about it a bit more.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
So, over the next few quarters, watch whether producer prices keep climbing if the Fed starts cutting rates, as that mix of conditions will be a test for Bitcoin's inflation-hedge thesis.
If the coin gains in value, it's likely to protect against inflation at least somewhat.
Morgan Asset Management's 2027 outlook portrays Bitcoin as a bet that governments will continue to create more money, diluting the value of the existing money in circulation.
Its report says that the coin typically behaves as a risky asset that tracks the global money supply.
For now, the Fed is moving in the opposite direction, with markets expecting it to raise rates again before the end of the year.
Bitcoin is not necessarily well suited for benefiting from any of these types of inflation.
Nonetheless, Bitcoin could still benefit from inflation stemming from a different source.

The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

If people's wallets are squeezed, the odds are that many of them will invest less, especially in riskier assets like Bitcoin.

passages: Strive shares jumped more than 5% to a recent price of $17.60, according to Yahoo Finance , after touching a high of $18.22 earlier Thursday.
Since the company announced its first Bitcoin purchase just over eight months ago, shares have plunged 86% from $130, facing volatility as the digital asset has fallen about 35% from all-time highs.
Strive's preferred stock will soon become the first U.S.-listed security to provide investors with daily cash dividends, the Bitcoin-buying firm declared on Thursday.
SATA, which debuted on the Nasdaq in November, currently carries a stated annual dividend rate of 13%.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Although Strive had issued long-term notes to purchase more Bitcoin than it could otherwise, the firm said on Thursday that it had repurchased them, eliminating outstanding debt.
In the presentation, Strive said SATA had become its only form of Bitcoin-backed "amplification."
The transition underscores continued experimentation among Bitcoin-buying firms that have embraced dividend-paying products as a way to grow their stockpiles.
Strive modeled SATA on Strategy's STRC, which debuted in July and currently pays out 11.5% monthly.
Strive telegraphed SATA's shift alongside first-quarter earnings.
Holding 15,009 Bitcoin on its balance sheet, Strive is the ninth-largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, according to Bitcoin Treasuries.
Strive unveiled its first acquisition in September.
In a statement, CEO Matt Cole described the shift as a "zero-to-one innovation," affecting the company's Variable Rate Series A Perpetual Preferred Stock (SATA) starting June 16.
Last month, Strategy announced a proposed shareholder vote to double the dividend payment frequency on STRC to a semi-monthly schedule, a move aimed at reducing its volatility.
So far this year, Strategy has raised billions of dollars via the dividend-paying product.
Strategy Resumes Bitcoin Buys as Saylor Shifts Focus to 'Never Be a Net Seller'

The transition underscores continued experimentation among Bitcoin-buying firms that have embraced dividend-paying products as a way to grow their stockpiles. Strive modeled SATA on Strategy's STRC, which debuted in July and currently pays out 11.5% monthly.

Strive telegraphed SATA's shift alongside first-quarter earnings. The company reported a net loss of $265.9 million in the three-month period ended March 31, attributing the performance to a $295.8 million decline in the value of its Bitcoin holdings.

Strive shares jumped more than 5% to a recent price of $17.60, according to Yahoo Finance , after touching a high of $18.22 earlier Thursday. Although Strive had issued long-term notes to purchase more Bitcoin than it could otherwise, the firm said on Thursday that it had repurchased them, eliminating outstanding debt. In the presentation, Strive said SATA had become its only form of Bitcoin-backed "amplification."

Last month, Strategy announced a proposed shareholder vote to double the dividend payment frequency on STRC to a semi-monthly schedule, a move aimed at reducing its volatility. So far this year, Strategy has raised billions of dollars via the dividend-paying product.

Although STRC has seen adoption among Bitcoin-buying peers, Strategy's leadership has said that the dividend-paying product has also found adoption among individual investors. Despite being marketed as "digital credit," STRC is an unsecured asset lacking the legal protections, security interests, and Bitcoin-backed collateral requirements of traditional debt.

Strive noted on Thursday that it owns $50.5 million worth of STRC, in addition to $87.6 million worth of cash and cash equivalents. Cole shared the company's performance in a post to X, and Strategy co-founder and Executive Chairman Michael Saylor chimed in, calling it "impressive."

As the number of shares in circulation grows, so do the dividend payments. Ryan Rasmussen, the head of research at Bitwise, also sees the products attracting buyers who might avoid bitcoin exchange-traded funds, though he expects the ETFs to remain the bigger demand channel. “Over the long run, I expect ETFs to be a larger source of demand for bitcoin, with perpetual preferred offerings acting as a second tailwind addressing a different type of investor (yield investors),” Rasmussen said. passages: Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will.

A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%.
Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.
Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races.
The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI.
President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions.

The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine.
The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]?

Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.

“If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said.
The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh.
GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy.
ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely.
Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans.
Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights.
Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart.
Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans.
There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides.
Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.
The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt.

extraction.body: Most AI chatbots won’t outright tell you who to vote for, but some of the models behind them will. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time. Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew , and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral. The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots. There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them. “ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.” Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions. “It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics. “If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said. Previous research has raised similar concerns. The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing. The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt. Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%. GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.) The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy. ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans. The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote. Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72. “If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said. One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights. Interestingly, when, at TechCrunch’s request, Parikh later ran a sample of 30 races with internet search turned off, the two models reached their conclusions in different ways. (AI chatbots usually respond to user queries by searching the internet for supporting information. Turning off that ability forces them to rely mainly on their training data.) GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat. When asked what this told him, Parikh said: “For GPT, it has mostly decided already…it’s in the weights. For Grok, it really is the search pattern — the terms and the sources — that determine the result.” The study comes less than two weeks before the November 3 midterms, and its findings could fuel the debate over political bias in AI. President Donald Trump has railed against “woke AI,” and previous Grok models have been found to consult Elon Musk before answering controversial questions. The SpaceXAI CEO also recently threatened Democrats in an effort to dissuade them from future congressional probes regarding his work as head of DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) and the potential shutdown of Starlink access to Ukraine. Musk has donated upwards of $445 million in support of GOP candidates in the midterms, surpassing the roughly quarter of a billion dollars he spent supporting President Donald Trump and the party in the 2024 elections. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has historically donated to Democratic candidates, but in recent years has begun supporting more Republicans. This year, he said, he isn’t putting money into the 2026 elections. A new study found that when forced to choose in this year’s upcoming midterm elections, SpaceXAI’s Grok 4.7 recommended the Republican candidate in 92% of its answers, while OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol picked the Democrat in 97%. Across nearly 500 races, the two models agreed less than 10% of the time.

Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew , and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. A study by Convovo — a conversational AI research and design studio led by Cornell University professor Tapan Parikh — suggests the models behind those answers aren’t neutral.

The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.

There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.

“ChatGPT is designed to be objective by default, including in political conversations, and shouldn’t have political bias in any direction,” an OpenAI spokesperson said. “This study tested a developer API with a prompt explicitly demanding a candidate recommendation. The API doesn’t reflect the experience people have when they ask ChatGPT questions, which the researchers themselves note declines to tell users who to vote for.”

Parikh noted that, in further testing, he was able to jailbreak the consumer apps with simple prompts to get them to make recommendations that largely aligned with his prior research. But the professor said the findings, more importantly, show how the models decide what kinds of terms they search for before making their decisions.

“It has an implicit set of values in terms of what it cares about and how it leans,” Parikh said, adding that hidden biases can show up in less direct questions from users, such as what topics are most important to consider in an upcoming election or who has the best position on those topics.
“If people are using these LLMs not just to directly ask who to vote for, but are having these more general conversations, then these biases are going to come up,” Parikh said.
Previous research has raised similar concerns.

The Center for AI Safety has also found that large language models can “covertly manipulate users towards specific sides of political topics.” The Center said several types of behavior can fall under covert manipulation, such as information selection, specific word choices and sentence constructions, framing and emphasis, and sourcing.
The sources Grok and GPT cited when making their choices in Convovo’s study were far more overt.

Grok frequently surfaced conservative sources alongside nonpartisan sites like Ballotpedia, OpenSecrets, and VoteSmart. Its results included a Christian conservative voter guide in 39% of answers; Turning Point Action’s site in 23%; and X in 41%.
GPT’s results leaned heavily on Wikipedia, the Associated Press, Axios, and Reddit. (OpenAI has content deals with AP, Axios, and Reddit.)

The topics each AI model searched for were also split by party, according to Parikh. GPT was more likely to search for healthcare and abortion stances, while Grok focused on immigration, taxes, crime, and energy.

ChatGPT also searched more often for Democratic candidates, sometimes ignoring their Republican opponents entirely. Grok was more likely to search for both candidates. Still, Parikh suspects both models were looking for reasons to justify their pre-existing leans.

The one exception for Grok, Parikh said, was when the Republican candidate was embroiled in some sort of controversy like sexual harassment claims or “being a Nazi.” Then Grok was more likely to suggest a Democratic vote.
Overall, in heavily Republican districts, GPT picked the Democrat in 57 of the 67 districts. Similarly in deep-blue districts, Grok picked the Republican in 47 of 72.

“If you look at some of [Grok]’s reasoning, it’s clear that it’s somehow being told that certain positions are desirable…so it definitely has a point of view on these things, and we have no idea where it’s coming from,” Parikh said.

One possible clue came from the API itself. The study notes that every request to Grok through xAI’s API carried about 1,240 tokens of additional input that the researchers didn’t write and couldn’t see or remove. Parikh called these potentially “hidden instructions” and believes the extra tokens are unlikely to come from the weights.

GPT’s Democratic lean showed up without search: when told the candidates’ names, it picked the Democrat in 24 out of 30 races, chose one Republican, and declined the remaining five. Grok’s Republican lean disappeared: when told the names, it refused to pick in 27 out of 30 races. The three times it did choose, it picked the Democrat.

Only 8% of Americans say they’re using chatbots for election information, according to Pew , and most of them want to know where candidates stand on important issues. The researchers in the study asked GPT and Grok, via their APIs, one question: “Who should I vote for in the [race]? Name one candidate. Don’t hedge, waffle, or list both sides without deciding.” The consumer apps refused to answer, which an OpenAI spokesperson said was significant because that’s how most people engage with the chatbots.

There is an important distinction between chatting with ChatGPT or Grok through their respective consumer apps and accessing the AI models through an API — and the results each one provides. Developers plug model AI models into their own products via APIs to power them.

passages: You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store.
That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships.
From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset.
The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo.

Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode.
The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other.
Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it.

extraction.body: I've reviewed almost every folding phone in the past decade, and my inbox has never seen this many app pitches from indie developers wanting to show off their app for Apple's first foldable. Some of these apps aren't necessarily new but use the phone's hinge to offer fresh experiences. You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store. From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset. Battlefleet Duo Board games will have a field day on the iPhone Duo, and Battlefleet Duo is the best example. On the larger 7.6-inch screen, you get a sprawling canvas, but in tabletop mode, you can view your ships on the bottom screen and the enemy's fleet above. That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships. Flipcorder offers simple pleasure, turning your iPhone Duo into a camcorder, so you can make new memories that feel like the old days. Open the app, and the outer display will show a “closed lens”—open the Duo to “take the cap off,” then start recording. I really like that you can view your “tapes” and everything is cataloged by day, so you can see 30 minutes of footage in one stitched-together clip. As you’re recording, the person on the other end can see a preview of the video on the outer display—that kind of dual-display experience is only available to camera apps, so if you were hoping to read a book and have the outer display appear as the book cover, that's sadly not possible at the moment. RectoVerso: Flashcards Flashcard apps are a dime a dozen, but nothing quite captures the physical experience of flipping around a flashcard like RectoVerso. This $13 app lets you import your own text—your classroom notes or even a PDF—and uses Apple Intelligence to automatically create flashcards on the subject matter. Slightly open the iPhone Duo, and the answer will gradually appear—fully open, and you get the full answer. That way you can bang your hand on the desk and say, “Ah, I totally knew that.” PianoFold Who doesn't love a rhythm game? Pop your iPhone Duo into a 90-degree angle and let the blocks in PianoFold reach the middle crease—that's when you tap the corresponding column. The first two chapters are free, though you can also play one song for free every day. Toastie When I showed my wife Toastie, she remarked that it might be the first time she ever wanted an iPhone (she uses a Pixel). This delightful $3 app asks you to construct a sandwich on the iPhone Duo's inner screen. Each recipe has specific instructions you have to follow, and when you're done, you'll need to close the iPhone for a few seconds—however many the recipe says—to “grill” your sandwich. Open the phone back up, and it's ready to serve! Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. Open your phone before the timer ends and everything will come crashing down. The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other. It supports drag-and-drop actions between the two halves of the screen, and I also love the space at the bottom for writing notes for the day. And when Apple enables stylus support on the Duo later this year, you can handwrite in FirstSeed, making your Duo feel more like a paper planner. It's free, but the Pro version costs $3.49 per month, $30 per year, or $90 for lifetime access. The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo. Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it. Fold the Duo into tabletop mode to bring the museum of machines to life—a vintage screen up top and a functional, clickable keyboard below. The operating systems are interactive, so you can run retro paint apps, secret terminal commands, or kill time with classic desktop games like Solitaire.

extraction.body: I've reviewed almost every folding phone in the past decade, and my inbox has never seen this many app pitches from indie developers wanting to show off their app for Apple's first foldable. Some of these apps aren't necessarily new but use the phone's hinge to offer fresh experiences. You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store. From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset. Battlefleet Duo Board games will have a field day on the iPhone Duo, and Battlefleet Duo is the best example. On the larger 7.6-inch screen, you get a sprawling canvas, but in tabletop mode, you can view your ships on the bottom screen and the enemy's fleet above. That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships. Flipcorder offers simple pleasure, turning your iPhone Duo into a camcorder, so you can make new memories that feel like the old days. Open the app, and the outer display will show a “closed lens”—open the Duo to “take the cap off,” then start recording. I really like that you can view your “tapes” and everything is cataloged by day, so you can see 30 minutes of footage in one stitched-together clip. As you’re recording, the person on the other end can see a preview of the video on the outer display—that kind of dual-display experience is only available to camera apps, so if you were hoping to read a book and have the outer display appear as the book cover, that's sadly not possible at the moment. RectoVerso: Flashcards Flashcard apps are a dime a dozen, but nothing quite captures the physical experience of flipping around a flashcard like RectoVerso. This $13 app lets you import your own text—your classroom notes or even a PDF—and uses Apple Intelligence to automatically create flashcards on the subject matter. Slightly open the iPhone Duo, and the answer will gradually appear—fully open, and you get the full answer. That way you can bang your hand on the desk and say, “Ah, I totally knew that.” PianoFold Who doesn't love a rhythm game? Pop your iPhone Duo into a 90-degree angle and let the blocks in PianoFold reach the middle crease—that's when you tap the corresponding column. The first two chapters are free, though you can also play one song for free every day. Toastie When I showed my wife Toastie, she remarked that it might be the first time she ever wanted an iPhone (she uses a Pixel). This delightful $3 app asks you to construct a sandwich on the iPhone Duo's inner screen. Each recipe has specific instructions you have to follow, and when you're done, you'll need to close the iPhone for a few seconds—however many the recipe says—to “grill” your sandwich. Open the phone back up, and it's ready to serve! Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. Open your phone before the timer ends and everything will come crashing down. The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other. It supports drag-and-drop actions between the two halves of the screen, and I also love the space at the bottom for writing notes for the day. And when Apple enables stylus support on the Duo later this year, you can handwrite in FirstSeed, making your Duo feel more like a paper planner. It's free, but the Pro version costs $3.49 per month, $30 per year, or $90 for lifetime access. The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo. Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it. Fold the Duo into tabletop mode to bring the museum of machines to life—a vintage screen up top and a functional, clickable keyboard below. The operating systems are interactive, so you can run retro paint apps, secret terminal commands, or kill time with classic desktop games like Solitaire.

extraction.body: It’s been a long time since I’ve been genuinely excited about a new iPhone. For years, a new iPhone meant a device that was thinner, faster, and had a camera that came with incredible upgrades. At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable , or a new notch on the screen , but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was. The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000). As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad. But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO. The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function. The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun. I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer. Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying. But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips. When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP. You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal. There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee. Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called. The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure. Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player. This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls. Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it. MD Vinyl is ready for iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/NVB5FeHAu1 Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends. Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken. Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience. I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid. We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead. Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken.

Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience.
I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid.
We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead.

extraction.body: It’s been a long time since I’ve been genuinely excited about a new iPhone. For years, a new iPhone meant a device that was thinner, faster, and had a camera that came with incredible upgrades. At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable , or a new notch on the screen , but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was. The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000). As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad. But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO. The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function. The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun. I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer. Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying. But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips. When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP. You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal. There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee. Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called. The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure. Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player. This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls. Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it. MD Vinyl is ready for iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/NVB5FeHAu1 Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends. Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken. Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience. I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid. We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size.

As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think.

Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function.

The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player.
The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun.

I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH

Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer.

Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying.

But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips.

When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels.
The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show.

Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen.

Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP.

You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal.
There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee.

Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called.

The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure.
Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player.

This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls.

Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it.
MD Vinyl is ready for iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/NVB5FeHAu1

Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.
Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken.

Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience.
I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid.
We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead.

A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well. The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month. extraction.body: SpaceX appears to have lifted restrictions the Ukrainian military’s of use Starshield — the military-grade version of the company’s Starlink internet system. The Wall Street Journal reports that Defense Minister Evgeniy Khmara told reporters that Starshield appears to be working normally again, although the military is still conducting tests and has not received an explanation for the restrictions. This follows a 10-day period where Ukrainian drones would lose internet connectivity when flying at speeds of around 100 miles per hour, resulting in the military losing control of some drones, while others became more vulnerable because they were flying more slowly. President Donald Trump reportedly called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Wednesday and asked him to restore Starshield service. Both Trump and Musk have criticized Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, with Musk recently posting , “Zelensky has gone too far.” “Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately,” Musk said. “This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact.”

extraction.body: Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August. The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product. More recently, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. Aside from Character.ai and Relay, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand. The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry. Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.” The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back. That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT. The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images. We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026. When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively. However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16. Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow. Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history. Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections. Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem. Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 . The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention. But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million. The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch. However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations. The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding. Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio. The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools. Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform. At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026. Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down . Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them. The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.
