The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”
The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.
We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.
Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.
However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.
Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.
The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai became a buzzed-about consumer AI app by letting people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

The trouble piled up after that. Families sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026. But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

sources.title: I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
passages: It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook.
After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh.

I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support.
My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive.
And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor.
Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs.

extraction.body: It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook. Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs. The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse. [Image: 2-in-1s can be seen as a weird compromise between laptops and tablets. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky. My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support.
My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive.
And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor.
Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs.

extraction.body: The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000). As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function. The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. With the Duo open, the cassette appears to play on the right side of the screen, next to album imagery on the right. When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman. The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech , which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech , like dumbphones , digital cameras, vinyl, CDs , and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives. Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun. Duo-Man is now Deck-Man! Expanding my app to have a unique experience on all platforms and not just the Duo, so it only makes sense to have a better name reflecting that. See you October 23 on the App Store! pic.twitter.com/kCdjcmbeGG The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed. Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut. You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. You can also draw and sketch to create colorful images that accompany your handwritten text, which makes it feel a lot more like using a real-life notebook as your journal or diary, and not some boring to-do app. The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun. I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer. For instance, when the Duo is open like a book, the view is split across the hinge with the movement game videos on the left, but when it’s open like a laptop, the videos shift to the vertical screen. You can also put it into tent mode, which is great for watching the videos with the Duo propped up on your desk. (Most people use Wakeout at work, when they take quick stretch breaks after sitting at a desk for too long.) If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display. Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying. But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips. When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP. You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal. There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee. Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called. The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure. Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player. This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls. Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it. MD Vinyl is ready for iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/NVB5FeHAu1 Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.

As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early.

Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech , which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech , like dumbphones , digital cameras, vinyl, CDs , and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives.
Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun.

Duo-Man is now Deck-Man! Expanding my app to have a unique experience on all platforms and not just the Duo, so it only makes sense to have a better name reflecting that. See you October 23 on the App Store! pic.twitter.com/kCdjcmbeGG

The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed.
Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut.

You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. (Most people use Wakeout at work, when they take quick stretch breaks after sitting at a desk for too long.)
If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display.

Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying.

But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips.

When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels.

Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called.

The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure.
Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player.

This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls.

Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it.
MD Vinyl is ready for iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/NVB5FeHAu1

Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.

extraction.body: The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000). As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early. Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple. Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV. The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size. As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think. Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function. The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player. With the Duo open, the cassette appears to play on the right side of the screen, next to album imagery on the right. When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman. The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech , which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech , like dumbphones , digital cameras, vinyl, CDs , and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives. Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun. Duo-Man is now Deck-Man! Expanding my app to have a unique experience on all platforms and not just the Duo, so it only makes sense to have a better name reflecting that. See you October 23 on the App Store! pic.twitter.com/kCdjcmbeGG The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed. Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut. You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. You can also draw and sketch to create colorful images that accompany your handwritten text, which makes it feel a lot more like using a real-life notebook as your journal or diary, and not some boring to-do app. The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun. I turned iPhone Duo into a real-life notebook where you can type anywhere in your own handwriting or with one of 12 fonts I designed myself. Type or draw, then close it. The next time you open the book, it shows your most recent note or the one captured nearest to your current… pic.twitter.com/d23kMbj8TH Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer. For instance, when the Duo is open like a book, the view is split across the hinge with the movement game videos on the left, but when it’s open like a laptop, the videos shift to the vertical screen. You can also put it into tent mode, which is great for watching the videos with the Duo propped up on your desk. (Most people use Wakeout at work, when they take quick stretch breaks after sitting at a desk for too long.) If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display. Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying. But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips. When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels. The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show. Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen. It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000).

As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early.
Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple.

Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV.

The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size.

Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function.

The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player.
With the Duo open, the cassette appears to play on the right side of the screen, next to album imagery on the right. When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman.

The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech , which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech , like dumbphones , digital cameras, vinyl, CDs , and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives.
Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun.

The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed.
Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut.

You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. You can also draw and sketch to create colorful images that accompany your handwritten text, which makes it feel a lot more like using a real-life notebook as your journal or diary, and not some boring to-do app.
The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun.

extraction.body: T he Socceroos star stares at the camera as he strides through an enormous atrium, the sound of his football boots on polished concrete echoing around him. Suddenly, he spawns four digital clones that peel off out of view to re-emerge in different settings around the world. This scene from a social media video is fake and generated by artificial intelligence. But it has been authorised by the very real 22-year-old footballer, Cristian Volpato, the latest professional athlete to licence and monetise his AI likeness. Draped in a white linen suit with his feet on the sand, Volpato’s “synthetic twin” turns towards a photographer as the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles tower behind him. Another dominates a large digital billboard wearing a football jersey. One smiles into a mirror while adjusting a sharp grey suit. This video was produced by a new company that acts as an AI licensing agent for professional athletes. Experts believe it is one small part of a nascent online industry that could transform the future of image rights and sports content. As bookmakers, broadcasters and brands increasingly use athletes’ images in AI generated content without their permission, some players are fighting back. In mid-September, Volpato, who plays for Italian Serie A club, Sassuolo, struck a deal with the California-based company Callandor to license his AI image. As part of the deal, Callandor was given exclusive rights to Volpato’s digital likeness, voice, biometric profiles and performance data. The company will monetise his AI image by landing brand deals, taking a cut, and help restrict content that does not have his approval. From Los Angeles, Callandor’s co-founder, Michael Fisk, tells Guardian Australia he’s in the business of making “synthetic twins”. “Cristian is constantly training,” Fisk says. “He’s constantly out there playing. If he has any free time whatsoever, he’ll probably want to spend it with family and friends, so he loses on a lot of opportunities on brand placements. “A synthetic twin could be used 24-7, year-round by brands. Assuming it’s approved, right?” Founded in February, Callandor has a small stable of athletes, including Brazilian footballer Jorginho and American sailor Chris Poole. Its campaigns are only in the pilot phase, but Callandor is pursuing an array of opportunities beyond traditional advertising. Fisk, a former executive at Sony Pictures and MGM, talks of creating AI-generated book voiceovers with foreign language editions. His team is also plotting apps that offer fans a personal relationship with a synthetic twin. “Ultimately, the holy grail of an athlete is to have that one-on-one interaction with fans,” Fisk says. He raises the prospect of creating an app that monitors how people play football. A digital clone of Volpato would give real-time instructions. “He’s realising I’m not handling the ball well [so] his synthetic twin can tell me, ‘Hey, you should be doing this and this and this’,” says Fisk. “Volpato would never be able to do that one-on-one with [them].” Volpato’s deal with Callandor is at the cutting edge of AI rights deals, but he isn’t the first to embrace the technology. In June, Brazilian superstar Neymar licensed his AI likeness to a Chinese-owned entertainment platform that created short videos published during the FIFA World Cup. These projects are being launched as governments across the world consider basic regulation of AI. At the moment, player contracts with major Australian sporting leagues make no mention of AI. But technology isn’t waiting for regulation to catch up and Fisk says his synthetic twin clients are blurring the lines between real and fake. “It’s becoming almost impossible to detect, that look and feel, the difference, particularly when you see it on a mobile device,” he says. William Saunders leads a small Sydney based start-up, Hyperknown, that’s trying to cut similar deals. He says athletes are beginning to realise that if they don’t monetise their AI image, others will. Earlier this month, the AFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of players without their consent. This was prompted by a complaint from the players’ union, which is considering whether stricter rules should be negotiated. “Sportsbet shows us what happens when companies and technology get ahead of consent,” Saunders says. “Volpato represents the counter-move: people establishing their rights before others start making decisions about their identities. “We’re watching a race between what technology can do and what people have actually authorised.” Many in the Australian sports industry, including content creators, bookmakers, broadcasters and athletes themselves, have started embracing the technology. Earlier this month, Australian cricketer Travis Head personally appeared in an ad for the broadcaster Kayo. He joked that his AI clone had already finished filming the ad, before throwing to vision of him riding a flying kookaburra . Brand deals and endorsements have become major money makers for athletes, with some securing multimillion dollar contracts. It remains unclear whether brands will be willing to pay as much for an AI clone, as opposed to the real deal. But Saunders, whose company has only just launched, says the opportunities are enormous. He talks of AI clones selling products in foreign languages in nations athletes have never visited. “The next trust signal won’t just say ‘made with AI’,” he says, referencing a tag often used by social media companies. “It will say ‘made with this person’s permission’. This has not slowed an explosion of deepfakes generated by increasingly sophisticated off-the-shelf software. In the UK last month, a campaign was launched by some the world’s top footballers, including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, which highlighted their concerns about deepfakes and the inability for regulation to slow their explosion. This campaign was backed by the global player union, Fifpro. One offshore casino used a deepfake video of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year .

extraction.body: T he Socceroos star stares at the camera as he strides through an enormous atrium, the sound of his football boots on polished concrete echoing around him. Suddenly, he spawns four digital clones that peel off out of view to re-emerge in different settings around the world. This scene from a social media video is fake and generated by artificial intelligence. But it has been authorised by the very real 22-year-old footballer, Cristian Volpato, the latest professional athlete to licence and monetise his AI likeness. Draped in a white linen suit with his feet on the sand, Volpato’s “synthetic twin” turns towards a photographer as the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles tower behind him. Another dominates a large digital billboard wearing a football jersey. One smiles into a mirror while adjusting a sharp grey suit. This video was produced by a new company that acts as an AI licensing agent for professional athletes. Experts believe it is one small part of a nascent online industry that could transform the future of image rights and sports content. As bookmakers, broadcasters and brands increasingly use athletes’ images in AI generated content without their permission, some players are fighting back. In mid-September, Volpato, who plays for Italian Serie A club, Sassuolo, struck a deal with the California-based company Callandor to license his AI image. As part of the deal, Callandor was given exclusive rights to Volpato’s digital likeness, voice, biometric profiles and performance data. The company will monetise his AI image by landing brand deals, taking a cut, and help restrict content that does not have his approval. From Los Angeles, Callandor’s co-founder, Michael Fisk, tells Guardian Australia he’s in the business of making “synthetic twins”. “Cristian is constantly training,” Fisk says. “He’s constantly out there playing. If he has any free time whatsoever, he’ll probably want to spend it with family and friends, so he loses on a lot of opportunities on brand placements. “A synthetic twin could be used 24-7, year-round by brands. Assuming it’s approved, right?” Founded in February, Callandor has a small stable of athletes, including Brazilian footballer Jorginho and American sailor Chris Poole. Its campaigns are only in the pilot phase, but Callandor is pursuing an array of opportunities beyond traditional advertising. Fisk, a former executive at Sony Pictures and MGM, talks of creating AI-generated book voiceovers with foreign language editions. His team is also plotting apps that offer fans a personal relationship with a synthetic twin. “Ultimately, the holy grail of an athlete is to have that one-on-one interaction with fans,” Fisk says. He raises the prospect of creating an app that monitors how people play football. A digital clone of Volpato would give real-time instructions. “He’s realising I’m not handling the ball well [so] his synthetic twin can tell me, ‘Hey, you should be doing this and this and this’,” says Fisk. “Volpato would never be able to do that one-on-one with [them].” Volpato’s deal with Callandor is at the cutting edge of AI rights deals, but he isn’t the first to embrace the technology. In June, Brazilian superstar Neymar licensed his AI likeness to a Chinese-owned entertainment platform that created short videos published during the FIFA World Cup. These projects are being launched as governments across the world consider basic regulation of AI. At the moment, player contracts with major Australian sporting leagues make no mention of AI. But technology isn’t waiting for regulation to catch up and Fisk says his synthetic twin clients are blurring the lines between real and fake. “It’s becoming almost impossible to detect, that look and feel, the difference, particularly when you see it on a mobile device,” he says. William Saunders leads a small Sydney based start-up, Hyperknown, that’s trying to cut similar deals. He says athletes are beginning to realise that if they don’t monetise their AI image, others will. Earlier this month, the AFL told its gambling partner Sportsbet to stop using AI images of players without their consent. This was prompted by a complaint from the players’ union, which is considering whether stricter rules should be negotiated. “Sportsbet shows us what happens when companies and technology get ahead of consent,” Saunders says. “Volpato represents the counter-move: people establishing their rights before others start making decisions about their identities. “We’re watching a race between what technology can do and what people have actually authorised.” Many in the Australian sports industry, including content creators, bookmakers, broadcasters and athletes themselves, have started embracing the technology. Earlier this month, Australian cricketer Travis Head personally appeared in an ad for the broadcaster Kayo. He joked that his AI clone had already finished filming the ad, before throwing to vision of him riding a flying kookaburra . Brand deals and endorsements have become major money makers for athletes, with some securing multimillion dollar contracts. It remains unclear whether brands will be willing to pay as much for an AI clone, as opposed to the real deal. But Saunders, whose company has only just launched, says the opportunities are enormous. He talks of AI clones selling products in foreign languages in nations athletes have never visited. “The next trust signal won’t just say ‘made with AI’,” he says, referencing a tag often used by social media companies. “It will say ‘made with this person’s permission’. This has not slowed an explosion of deepfakes generated by increasingly sophisticated off-the-shelf software. In the UK last month, a campaign was launched by some the world’s top footballers, including Cole Palmer and Lucy Bronze, which highlighted their concerns about deepfakes and the inability for regulation to slow their explosion. This campaign was backed by the global player union, Fifpro. One offshore casino used a deepfake video of Manchester United player Bruno Fernandes in advertising earlier this year .

The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield. According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement: “Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. sources.title: Agent cloud startup Daytona hits $1B valuation backed by FirstMark and a who’s who of angels
passages: The New York-based startup has attracted not just FirstMark (which also led its $24 million Series A in February), but also a host of well-known angels in this latest round.

Daytona says they include Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Zoom’s Eric Yuan, Datadog’s Olivier Pomel, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo (who is also an OpenAI board member), and Mercor’s Brendan Foody.
It also names Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next, and Okta Ventures as participants.

Three-year-old Daytona is building a cloud specifically for long-running agents, which have different infrastructure needs than yesteryear’s software, the startup contends. “Agents don’t work like the long-lived services today’s cloud was designed for.
They spin up thousands of short, stateful jobs nobody planned in advance, and they need a cloud built for that,” founder Ivan Burazin wrote in a blog post announcing the new round .
Daytona Platforms announced on Friday that it had raised a $60 million Series B round at a $1 billion valuation led by FirstMark Growth.

passages: BBC’s Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots.
sources.body: BBC’s Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots.

extraction.body: BBC’s Blue Planet III is looking to prove its authenticity by leaving in the less-than-perfect shots. Previous incarnations of the nature series were defined by their gorgeous, crystal-clear footage that seemed almost too good to be real. To counter that, Blue Planet III goes warts and all. Executive Producer Elizabeth White told The Guardian in the past, “the amount of plankton and things” floating in the water would have caused them to cut a shot. Or “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’” Instead, this time they’re leaving it all in to show a more authentic, organic version of the oceans. White says that real ocean creatures “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine.”

As technology companies spend hundreds of billions of dollars each year on data centers, semiconductors, and other power infrastructure, investors are wondering whether the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution can sustain its momentum. What happens if AI spending slows? Or if businesses realize that their investments aren't generating the returns they expected? Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » These are important questions, especially for investors looking to buy stocks and hold them for decades. Warren Buffett built his fortune by choosing companies with durable competitive advantages, predictable earnings, and management teams capable of allocating capital wisely. Rather than speculating on the next technological breakthrough , Buffett prefers companies that thrive across different economic cycles. Two stocks in Berkshire Hathaway 's portfolio fit those criteria particularly well: Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG). While both companies stand to benefit from AI, their investment cases do not depend entirely on the technology succeeding. Berkshire first started investing in Apple in 2016, long before generative AI became Wall Street's favorite investment theme. At the time, Buffett recognized something most investors were discounting: Apple wasn't simply a hardware manufacturer. The company had acquired an extremely loyal customer base, possessed a powerful brand, and built a product ecosystem that kept customers sticky. That combination creates what Buffett calls an economic moat, a durable competitive advantage that helps a company protect its profits. Nearly a decade later, Apple's business remains remarkably resilient. Instead of creating a new product every few years, Apple has found different ways to monetize its platform. For example, the company's Services segment includes the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, AppleCare, and other offerings that generate recurring revenue from Apple's installed base of billions of devices worldwide. This is highly attractive because Apple's customers do not need to purchase a new iPhone every year for the company to generate incremental revenue. What makes Apple so different from other speculative AI investments is that the company doesn't really need AI to become its largest revenue source. Sure, AI can strengthen Apple's products and encourage customers to upgrade. But the company's established hardware business, expanding services ecosystem, and powerful brand already support substantial earnings and cash flow. Moreover, Apple also consistently returns capital to shareholders through stock buybacks and dividends, another characteristic Buffett appreciates. Although Berkshire has reduced its Apple position over time, the stock remains its largest holding. That continued exposure underscores the enduring appeal of Apple stock. Berkshire first disclosed a position in Alphabet in November 2025 and has since added to it over the past year. Like Apple, Alphabet has many characteristics associated with Buffett's investment philosophy. The company owns two of the world's most recognizable brands, Google and YouTube, both of which boast highly profitable advertising businesses. Indeed, AI is becoming an important growth driver for Alphabet as the company integrates its Gemini AI models into Search, Workspace, Android, and Google Cloud. Nevertheless, Alphabet isn't a pure-play AI company. Google Search, YouTube, subscription services, and cloud computing already represented enormous businesses with established customer bases. AI simply enhances their capabilities, but Alphabet doesn't need to build an entirely new platform to justify its long-term potential. The biggest risk facing AI investors isn't that the technology fails. It's that investors overestimate how much money individual companies will make from it. History is filled with examples of promising technologies that transformed society without generating attractive returns for each company involved. This is what makes Apple and Alphabet compelling. Both companies have diversified business models, recognizable brands, significant competitive advantages, and established sources of recurring cash flow. They also have the financial flexibility to invest in AI without depending entirely on that infrastructure for their survival. For investors seeking AI stocks to buy and hold forever, I see Apple and Alphabet as prime examples. Their existing businesses already generate attractive growth, while AI merely offers an additional tailwind. That combination resembles the kind of long-term investment Buffett has favored throughout his legendary career. Before you buy stock in Alphabet, consider this: The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Alphabet wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years. sources.title: Should You Sell Your Stocks if a Bear Market Is Coming? Here's Warren Buffett's Advice. - AOL.com
passages: If you're thinking about selling stocks to outrun a future bear market , let's look at wisdom from Warren Buffett.
His timeless advice should hopefully inspire the rest of us to avoid trying to "time the market."
No one knows if a bear market is really coming, or how long it will last, or when it will end, or how rapid the eventual recovery in the S&P 500 might be.
Even Warren Buffett himself frequently spoke humbly about how unpredictable and unknowable the day-to-day, month-to-month and year-to-year moves in stock market prices could be.
Here's the problem: timing the market doesn't work.
If you sell stocks right before a crash, you might miss out on the recovery.
The stocks you sell today might suddenly be more expensive when you're ready to buy back into the market.
You don't have to pick stocks like Warren Buffett to get rich.
From 1964 to 2024, Buffett earned a compound annual growth rate of about 19.9%.
Warren Buffett was a long-term investor who preferred to hold stocks “forever.”
Buffett has famously said that his favorite holding period (how long to wait to sell a stock after buying) was "forever."

extraction.body: As technology companies spend hundreds of billions of dollars each year on data centers, semiconductors, and other power infrastructure, investors are wondering whether the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution can sustain its momentum. What happens if AI spending slows? Or if businesses realize that their investments aren't generating the returns they expected? These are important questions, especially for investors looking to buy stocks and hold them for decades. Warren Buffett built his fortune by choosing companies with durable competitive advantages, predictable earnings, and management teams capable of allocating capital wisely. Rather than speculating on the next technological breakthrough , Buffett prefers companies that thrive across different economic cycles. Two stocks in Berkshire Hathaway 's portfolio fit those criteria particularly well: Apple ( AAPL -0.14% ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL -1.24% ) ( GOOG -1.08% ) . While both companies stand to benefit from AI, their investment cases do not depend entirely on the technology succeeding. Berkshire first started investing in Apple in 2016, long before generative AI became Wall Street's favorite investment theme. At the time, Buffett recognized something most investors were discounting: Apple wasn't simply a hardware manufacturer. The company had acquired an extremely loyal customer base, possessed a powerful brand, and built a product ecosystem that kept customers sticky. That combination creates what Buffett calls an economic moat , a durable competitive advantage that helps a company protect its profits. Nearly a decade later, Apple's business remains remarkably resilient. Instead of creating a new product every few years, Apple has found different ways to monetize its platform. For example, the company's Services segment includes the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, AppleCare, and other offerings that generate recurring revenue from Apple's installed base of billions of devices worldwide. This is highly attractive because Apple's customers do not need to purchase a new iPhone every year for the company to generate incremental revenue. What makes Apple so different from other speculative AI investments is that the company doesn't really need AI to become its largest revenue source. Sure, AI can strengthen Apple's products and encourage customers to upgrade. But the company's established hardware business, expanding services ecosystem, and powerful brand already support substantial earnings and cash flow. Moreover, Apple also consistently returns capital to shareholders through stock buybacks and dividends, another characteristic Buffett appreciates. Although Berkshire has reduced its Apple position over time, the stock remains its largest holding. That continued exposure underscores the enduring appeal of Apple stock. Warren Buffett, former CEO and chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. Image source: Getty Images. Berkshire first disclosed a position in Alphabet in November 2025 and has since added to it over the past year. Like Apple, Alphabet has many characteristics associated with Buffett's investment philosophy . The company owns two of the world's most recognizable brands, Google and YouTube, both of which boast highly profitable advertising businesses. Indeed, AI is becoming an important growth driver for Alphabet as the company integrates its Gemini AI models into Search, Workspace, Android, and Google Cloud. Nevertheless, Alphabet isn't a pure-play AI company. Google Search, YouTube, subscription services, and cloud computing already represented enormous businesses with established customer bases. AI simply enhances their capabilities, but Alphabet doesn't need to build an entirely new platform to justify its long-term potential. The biggest risk facing AI investors isn't that the technology fails. It's that investors overestimate how much money individual companies will make from it. History is filled with examples of promising technologies that transformed society without generating attractive returns for each company involved. This is what makes Apple and Alphabet compelling. Both companies have diversified business models , recognizable brands, significant competitive advantages, and established sources of recurring cash flow. They also have the financial flexibility to invest in AI without depending entirely on that infrastructure for their survival. For investors seeking AI stocks to buy and hold forever, I see Apple and Alphabet as prime examples. Their existing businesses already generate attractive growth, while AI merely offers an additional tailwind. That combination resembles the kind of long-term investment Buffett has favored throughout his legendary career. Adam Spatacco has positions in Alphabet. Two stocks in Berkshire Hathaway 's portfolio fit those criteria particularly well: Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG). At the time, Buffett recognized something most investors were discounting: Apple wasn't simply a hardware manufacturer. The company had acquired an extremely loyal customer base, possessed a powerful brand, and built a product ecosystem that kept customers sticky. That combination creates what Buffett calls an economic moat, a durable competitive advantage that helps a company protect its profits. Nearly a decade later, Apple's business remains remarkably resilient. Instead of creating a new product every few years, Apple has found different ways to monetize its platform. For example, the company's Services segment includes the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, AppleCare, and other offerings that generate recurring revenue from Apple's installed base of billions of devices worldwide. Sure, AI can strengthen Apple's products and encourage customers to upgrade. But the company's established hardware business, expanding services ecosystem, and powerful brand already support substantial earnings and cash flow. Moreover, Apple also consistently returns capital to shareholders through stock buybacks and dividends, another characteristic Buffett appreciates. If you're thinking about selling stocks to outrun a future bear market , let's look at wisdom from Warren Buffett. His timeless advice should hopefully inspire the rest of us to avoid trying to "time the market." In more than 60 years as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) , Buffett earned an astonishing total return of 5.5 million percent. But he didn't do this by day trading or speculation, betting on short-term moves in the market, or flipping meme stocks for a quick profit. Instead, Buffett was a long-term investor. He bought the stocks of high-quality companies that had sustainable, understandable business models. He backed company leaders that he believed in. And he held onto those winning stocks for years or decades. Buffett has famously said that his favorite holding period (how long to wait to sell a stock after buying) was "forever." Buy-and-hold investing is the antidote to short-term stock market anxiety. It's understandable that people feel nervous about the latest headlines. The economy is always uncertain. The stock market is often volatile. But for most people, once you've decided to put your money to work in the stock market, it's best to just leave that money alone and stay invested -- through good times and bad. When people try to sell stocks "before the bear market starts," or when people wait to buy more stocks "until next month, after the market calms down," this is called "timing the market." It means people believe they know better than the rest of us what's going to happen in the future. It's a way of trying to avoid the pain of stock market losses, while enjoying only the upside after stocks bounce back. Here's the problem: timing the market doesn't work. If you sell stocks right before a crash, you might miss out on the recovery. The S&P 500 might drop 1% in a day, 5% in a month, or 20% (or more) in a year. But it can bounce back even faster. The stocks you sell today might suddenly be more expensive when you're ready to buy back into the market. What about the days when the S&P 500 goes up by 1% or 2%? What about the months when it goes up by 5% or more? If you're trying to time the market and guess the future, you might not have your money invested during those times of maximum gains. Missing out on just a few of those best-performing days can hurt your long-term wealth in surprising ways. A study from Schwab found that, based on 20 years of S&P 500 historical returns from 2005 to 2024, the S&P 500 delivered annualized total returns of 10.3%. But investors who missed out on the top 10 days during those 20 years only gained 6.1% annualized returns. That's a reduction of about 40%. Trying to time the market often leaves people hustling backward. Beyond the math, another big problem with timing the market is mindset. The frailties of human nature and the limits of psychology are tough to overcome. Many people overestimate how savvy, decisive, and mentally strong they'll be during a stock market crisis. Bear markets are stressful. People often don't feel great about their finances when the S&P 500 is down 10% or more. Even if you manage to sell stocks at "the right time," how do you know when to buy the dip and get back into the market? Do you really think you'll be level-headed and confident enough to buy stocks at just the right moment? Instead of being courageous, swashbuckling stock market heroes, many people tend to get more fearful and risk-averse during bear markets. They might think, "Oh no, a recession is coming, the economy is collapsing, I might lose my job, I'd better hold onto every dollar of my spare cash!" As a result, they miss out on big opportunities to buy stocks at a discount. No one can predict the future; if they could, they'd be richer than Buffett. Even Warren Buffett himself frequently spoke humbly about how unpredictable and unknowable the day-to-day, month-to-month and year-to-year moves in stock market prices could be. He didn't claim to know what was going to happen next with the S&P 500 in the short term. But he believed that in the long term, buying stocks -- and holding onto them, not panic-selling in a bear market -- was the best path to build wealth. You don't have to pick stocks like Warren Buffett to get rich. From 1964 to 2024, Buffett earned a compound annual growth rate of about 19.9%. But the S&P 500 index achieved 10.4% returns during those 60 years. extraction.body: As technology companies spend hundreds of billions of dollars each year on data centers, semiconductors, and other power infrastructure, investors are wondering whether the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution can sustain its momentum. What happens if AI spending slows? Or if businesses realize that their investments aren't generating the returns they expected? These are important questions, especially for investors looking to buy stocks and hold them for decades. Warren Buffett built his fortune by choosing companies with durable competitive advantages, predictable earnings, and management teams capable of allocating capital wisely. Rather than speculating on the next technological breakthrough , Buffett prefers companies that thrive across different economic cycles. Two stocks in Berkshire Hathaway 's portfolio fit those criteria particularly well: Apple ( AAPL -0.14% ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL -1.24% ) ( GOOG -1.08% ) . While both companies stand to benefit from AI, their investment cases do not depend entirely on the technology succeeding. Berkshire first started investing in Apple in 2016, long before generative AI became Wall Street's favorite investment theme. At the time, Buffett recognized something most investors were discounting: Apple wasn't simply a hardware manufacturer. The company had acquired an extremely loyal customer base, possessed a powerful brand, and built a product ecosystem that kept customers sticky. That combination creates what Buffett calls an economic moat , a durable competitive advantage that helps a company protect its profits. Nearly a decade later, Apple's business remains remarkably resilient. Instead of creating a new product every few years, Apple has found different ways to monetize its platform. For example, the company's Services segment includes the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, AppleCare, and other offerings that generate recurring revenue from Apple's installed base of billions of devices worldwide. This is highly attractive because Apple's customers do not need to purchase a new iPhone every year for the company to generate incremental revenue. What makes Apple so different from other speculative AI investments is that the company doesn't really need AI to become its largest revenue source. Sure, AI can strengthen Apple's products and encourage customers to upgrade. But the company's established hardware business, expanding services ecosystem, and powerful brand already support substantial earnings and cash flow. Moreover, Apple also consistently returns capital to shareholders through stock buybacks and dividends, another characteristic Buffett appreciates. Although Berkshire has reduced its Apple position over time, the stock remains its largest holding. That continued exposure underscores the enduring appeal of Apple stock. Warren Buffett, former CEO and chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. Image source: Getty Images. Berkshire first disclosed a position in Alphabet in November 2025 and has since added to it over the past year. Like Apple, Alphabet has many characteristics associated with Buffett's investment philosophy . The company owns two of the world's most recognizable brands, Google and YouTube, both of which boast highly profitable advertising businesses. Indeed, AI is becoming an important growth driver for Alphabet as the company integrates its Gemini AI models into Search, Workspace, Android, and Google Cloud. Nevertheless, Alphabet isn't a pure-play AI company. Google Search, YouTube, subscription services, and cloud computing already represented enormous businesses with established customer bases. AI simply enhances their capabilities, but Alphabet doesn't need to build an entirely new platform to justify its long-term potential. The biggest risk facing AI investors isn't that the technology fails. It's that investors overestimate how much money individual companies will make from it. History is filled with examples of promising technologies that transformed society without generating attractive returns for each company involved. This is what makes Apple and Alphabet compelling. Both companies have diversified business models , recognizable brands, significant competitive advantages, and established sources of recurring cash flow. They also have the financial flexibility to invest in AI without depending entirely on that infrastructure for their survival. For investors seeking AI stocks to buy and hold forever, I see Apple and Alphabet as prime examples. Their existing businesses already generate attractive growth, while AI merely offers an additional tailwind. That combination resembles the kind of long-term investment Buffett has favored throughout his legendary career. Adam Spatacco has positions in Alphabet. passages: Following the launch of the HomeView and other smart home products last week , Apple has now confirmed its third product event of the season .
Invitations bearing the tagline "Pro and Tell" went out this week, and the showcase will take place on October 28 in Los Angeles.
However, it won't be a traditional event, but rather a briefing for the press and creators.
As usual, Apple doesn't reveal in advance which products it will announce, but all signs point to two main categories: Mac and iPad.
If the rumors are true, we'll see the first MacBook with an OLED display and touchscreen, and the M6 chip coming to more Macs.
Here's everything to expect from next week's event.
Another upgrade should be the A20 Pro chip, which is already in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo.
Other rumors about the new iPad mini include thinner bezels around the screen, a relocated front-facing camera and some level of water resistance for the first time.
Gurman's sources claimed that Apple will stick with the current M5 Pro and M5 Max, rather than switching to the M6 family.
This Mac won't come cheap either, according to a report by Macworld .
The current models without touchscreens should remain available for those not wanting to pay the higher price.
The iPad mini is also expected to get some spotlight with a new generation, and this will be a big one, too.
The leading candidate is the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro — Apple did something similar last year with the M5 version .
Don't expect a touchscreen, OLED display or any design changes in this version, though.
