extraction.body: From the first touchscreen MacBook to an OLED iPad mini, here's everything Apple is expected to announce next week. Following the launch of the HomeView and other smart home products last week , Apple has now confirmed its third product event of the season . Invitations bearing the tagline "Pro and Tell" went out this week, and the showcase will take place on October 28 in Los Angeles. However, it won't be a traditional event, but rather a briefing for the press and creators. As usual, Apple doesn't reveal in advance which products it will announce, but all signs point to two main categories: Mac and iPad. If the rumors are true, we'll see the first MacBook with an OLED display and touchscreen, and the M6 chip coming to more Macs. In addition, the iPad mini might also get a major update with an OLED display and a faster chip. Here's everything to expect from next week's event. The star of the show is expected to be a new MacBook Pro, which will is supposed to be the first Mac with a touchscreen. Rumors suggest it will come in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes like the current models — but they may end up looking quite different. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman recently reported that this new MacBook could be thinner and lighter, while the OLED display should allow for thinner bezels and a hole-punch camera cutout with a Dynamic Island instead of a notch. Chances are this will be the biggest redesign of the MacBook Pro since the versions that were introduced in 2021. However, don't expect to see the new M6 chip inside it. Gurman's sources claimed that Apple will stick with the current M5 Pro and M5 Max, rather than switching to the M6 family. If you were hoping for a faster MacBook Pro, you'll likely have to wait until 2027, when Apple is rumored to refresh its high-end laptop with the M7 Pro and M7 Max chips. This Mac won't come cheap either, according to a report by Macworld . It probably won't be a successor to existing models, but rather an even more expensive version that expands the lineup. The current models without touchscreens should remain available for those not wanting to pay the higher price. Although the touchscreen MacBook won't get the M6 chip, other Macs will. The M6 was introduced in August with the latest Mac mini , and now other Macs are rumored to be getting it as well. The leading candidate is the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro — Apple did something similar last year with the M5 version . Don't expect a touchscreen, OLED display or any design changes in this version, though. The only upgrade should be the M6 chip, which offers improved performance and lower power consumption. The iMac is also a strong candidate for an update next week, especially since the current model was introduced in 2024 and still runs on the M4 chip . Here, the M6 chip is expected to mark an even more significant jump, with much better CPU and GPU performance. The M6 also comes with a dual 16-core Neural Engine, which runs AI tasks much faster. We may also see new color options available, although the design will remain the same. Macs likely won't be the only products getting an update at next week's event. The iPad mini is also expected to get some spotlight with a new generation, and this will be a big one, too. Apple is reportedly adding an OLED display to the iPad mini for the first time. Current models still have LCD screens. If true, the mini will be the first iPad besides the iPad Pro to feature an OLED display. Another upgrade should be the A20 Pro chip, which is already in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Currently, the iPad mini still runs on the A17 Pro chip from the iPhone 15 Pro — and is known for heating up a lot . Other rumors about the new iPad mini include thinner bezels around the screen, a relocated front-facing camera and some level of water resistance for the first time. Of course, none of these details have been confirmed yet, so we'll find out what Apple has to share for sure on October 28.

passages: Apple marketing chief Greg Joswiak on Monday shared a short teaser video and the message “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week,” confirming the company’s next product experience for Wednesday, October 28th, in Los Angeles.

The animated clip shows the Apple logo forming from flowing, multi-colored light trails against a black background — a stylized nod to the event’s “Pro and tell” tagline. Joswiak’s post, which quickly drew thousands of likes and shares, follows the recent distribution of media invites for an in-person gathering starting at 10 a.m. PT.
— Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) October 19, 2026

This marks Apple’s second hardware-focused experience of the month. On October 13th in New York, the company introduced the HomeView smart display, HomePod mini 2, and an updated Apple TV 4K under the “Welcome home” banner. The October 28 gathering in Los Angeles is expected to follow a similar hands-on format for select media and creators rather than a traditional livestreamed keynote, with product announcements and videos likely timed to the event.
Expected Lineup Centers on Mac and iPad Upgrades
While Apple has not confirmed specific products, reporting from Bloomberg News ’ Mark Gurman and coverage across tech outlets points to a Mac- and iPad-focused slate:

• Redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreens (Apple’s first on a Mac), a Dynamic Island cutout replacing the notch, and a significantly lighter design. These are widely expected to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than a new M6 Pro/Max generation.
• An entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro and a refreshed iMac powered by the M6 chip, largely retaining current designs.
• A new iPad mini with an OLED display, a relocated landscape-oriented FaceTime camera, and an updated speaker system.

Gurman has indicated the devices could be introduced around October 28th, with availability potentially following in early November (reports have referenced a possible November 6th window tied to retail preparations). Earlier speculation about a “MacBook Ultra” name appears to have been walked back, with the touchscreen models expected to remain in the MacBook Pro lineup.

The prospect of a touchscreen MacBook Pro represents a significant departure for Apple, which has long argued against touch input on traditional laptops in favor of trackpad and keyboard precision. An OLED panel would also mark a display upgrade from the mini-LED technology in recent high-end Pros, promising better contrast, blacks, and brightness alongside the new interaction model and software support (reports have referenced testing with macOS versions that include finger input handling).

Joswiak’s playful wording and the fluid logo animation have fueled speculation that the teaser alludes to the tactile or visual qualities of the expected OLED touchscreen machines. Apple’s fall product cadence has been busy, following recent iPhone and related launches, and the “Pro and tell” experience appears positioned as a focused showcase for professional and creative users.
Official details will arrive next week. Until then, the combination of confirmed event timing and consistent high-level reporting has set clear expectations for Apple’s next major hardware step.

That’s according to Apple’s Greg Joswiak, who posted a short teaser on Monday with the line “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.” The tagline is “Pro and Tell,” and media invites are already out. MacStories editor Federico Viticci shared his invite, confirming the date as October 28 in Los Angeles. Joswiak’s post also included a short glowing Apple logo video that matches the invite art. This isn’t the usual Apple Park livestream setup. Reporters are being brought to L.A. for an in-person experience, similar to the recent Welcome Home smart home launch. The invite says things kick off at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET, which is when we should see the first product details land. What shows up is still rumour territory, but the expectations line up with recent Apple Store resets and earlier leaks. Treat all of that as unconfirmed until Apple says otherwise. Canadian shoppers won’t get local pricing until launch day, but if past Pro refreshes are any guide, expect a familiar sticker shock and a week of “should I wait” debates in the comments. extraction.body: From the first touchscreen MacBook to an OLED iPad mini, here's everything Apple is expected to announce next week. Following the launch of the HomeView and other smart home products last week , Apple has now confirmed its third product event of the season . Invitations bearing the tagline "Pro and Tell" went out this week, and the showcase will take place on October 28 in Los Angeles. However, it won't be a traditional event, but rather a briefing for the press and creators. As usual, Apple doesn't reveal in advance which products it will announce, but all signs point to two main categories: Mac and iPad. If the rumors are true, we'll see the first MacBook with an OLED display and touchscreen, and the M6 chip coming to more Macs. In addition, the iPad mini might also get a major update with an OLED display and a faster chip. Here's everything to expect from next week's event. The star of the show is expected to be a new MacBook Pro, which will is supposed to be the first Mac with a touchscreen. Rumors suggest it will come in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes like the current models — but they may end up looking quite different. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman recently reported that this new MacBook could be thinner and lighter, while the OLED display should allow for thinner bezels and a hole-punch camera cutout with a Dynamic Island instead of a notch. Chances are this will be the biggest redesign of the MacBook Pro since the versions that were introduced in 2021. However, don't expect to see the new M6 chip inside it. Gurman's sources claimed that Apple will stick with the current M5 Pro and M5 Max, rather than switching to the M6 family. If you were hoping for a faster MacBook Pro, you'll likely have to wait until 2027, when Apple is rumored to refresh its high-end laptop with the M7 Pro and M7 Max chips. This Mac won't come cheap either, according to a report by Macworld . It probably won't be a successor to existing models, but rather an even more expensive version that expands the lineup. The current models without touchscreens should remain available for those not wanting to pay the higher price. Although the touchscreen MacBook won't get the M6 chip, other Macs will. The M6 was introduced in August with the latest Mac mini , and now other Macs are rumored to be getting it as well. The leading candidate is the entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro — Apple did something similar last year with the M5 version . Don't expect a touchscreen, OLED display or any design changes in this version, though. The only upgrade should be the M6 chip, which offers improved performance and lower power consumption. The iMac is also a strong candidate for an update next week, especially since the current model was introduced in 2024 and still runs on the M4 chip . Here, the M6 chip is expected to mark an even more significant jump, with much better CPU and GPU performance. The M6 also comes with a dual 16-core Neural Engine, which runs AI tasks much faster. We may also see new color options available, although the design will remain the same. Macs likely won't be the only products getting an update at next week's event. The iPad mini is also expected to get some spotlight with a new generation, and this will be a big one, too. Apple is reportedly adding an OLED display to the iPad mini for the first time. Current models still have LCD screens. If true, the mini will be the first iPad besides the iPad Pro to feature an OLED display. Another upgrade should be the A20 Pro chip, which is already in the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo. Currently, the iPad mini still runs on the A17 Pro chip from the iPhone 15 Pro — and is known for heating up a lot . Other rumors about the new iPad mini include thinner bezels around the screen, a relocated front-facing camera and some level of water resistance for the first time. Of course, none of these details have been confirmed yet, so we'll find out what Apple has to share for sure on October 28.

• Redesigned 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreens (Apple’s first on a Mac), a Dynamic Island cutout replacing the notch, and a significantly lighter design. These are widely expected to use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips rather than a new M6 Pro/Max generation.

• A new iPad mini with an OLED display, a relocated landscape-oriented FaceTime camera, and an updated speaker system.

Earlier speculation about a “MacBook Ultra” name appears to have been walked back, with the touchscreen models expected to remain in the MacBook Pro lineup.

Joswiak’s playful wording and the fluid logo animation have fueled speculation that the teaser alludes to the tactile or visual qualities of the expected OLED touchscreen machines. Apple’s fall product cadence has been busy, following recent iPhone and related launches, and the “Pro and tell” experience appears positioned as a focused showcase for professional and creative users.
Official details will arrive next week. Until then, the combination of confirmed event timing and consistent high-level reporting has set clear expectations for Apple’s next major hardware step.

ChatGPT and DeepSeek predict XRP outperforms Bitcoin through year-end because XRP's smaller market cap amplifies ETF inflows faster and the CLARITY Act proposes federal commodity classification for XRP.
XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) trades near $1.40 after falling 62% from its July 2025 peak of $3.65.
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) sits around $66,000, down 48% from October's $126,000 high.

On the Bitcoin side, ChatGPT projects $110,000–$150,000 as its base, or roughly 65–125% from $66,000.
When asked directly where to put $10,000 between XRP and Bitcoin, ChatGPT picked XRP—citing catalysts that are already active versus Bitcoin still waiting on the Fed.
But the catalysts each model weighs are different.
ChatGPT's XRP price prediction assumes these catalysts keep building without needing a new breakthrough to push prices higher.
DeepSeek takes a much more aggressive stance on XRP.
For Bitcoin, DeepSeek is notably more cautious—its most recent projection targets $100,000 by year-end after a potential drop to $41,000 during Q2 or Q3.

DeepSeek treats XRP's 2026 selloff as temporary noise driven by macro headwinds rather than any weakness in the token's fundamentals, while viewing Bitcoin's recovery as dependent on a reflationary second half.
A wider Iran conflict pushing oil past $90 and a hawkish Fed under Kevin Warsh signaling no cuts in 2026 could send Bitcoin below $60,000—and XRP would take a harder hit.
Institutional ETF holders already pulled $6 billion out of BTC funds in early 2026, and another wave of selling could drag XRP toward $0.90–$1.10 while Bitcoin holds $50,000–$60,000.

Both models agree XRP would beat Bitcoin's gains, but the difference in ROI margins boils down to the catalysts each AI takes into consideration. XRP's $85 billion market cap is roughly 15x smaller than Bitcoin's $1.3 trillion, so the same dollar of ETF capital moves the XRP price significantly more. XRP ETFs pulled in $1.24 billion since November while BTC ETFs bled over $6 billion, and both AI models use that split as the starting point for why XRP wins on returns. But the catalysts each model weighs are different. ChatGPT leans on what's already working—ETF inflows are steady, Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin crossed $1 billion in market cap within its first year, and BNY Mellon is already custodying it for institutional clients. ChatGPT's XRP price prediction assumes these catalysts keep building without needing a new breakthrough to push prices higher. DeepSeek prices in what hasn't happened yet. The CLARITY Act — which would classify XRP as a digital commodity under federal law—is the big one. Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse puts the odds of passage by April at 80%, and JPMorgan analysts identified eight provisions in the bill that could reshape crypto markets if it clears the Senate by mid-year. DeepSeek also factors in Ripple's conditional OCC banking charter and a potential Federal Reserve master account, which would let Ripple hold RLUSD reserves directly at the central bank. If even half of these land, the XRP price is looking at a very different ceiling than where it sits today. The risk is that none of these catalysts are guaranteed, and the XRP price has shown exactly how fragile it gets when sentiment turns. XRP is down 26% year-to-date while Bitcoin has only lost 17% over the same stretch, and on March 2 alone, $652 million in XRP hit Binance as the Iran escalation rattled markets. Open interest on XRP derivatives has collapsed 70% since October, dropping from $660 million to $203 million, which means there's a lot less sitting between the current price and a sharp move in either direction. AI predictions also shift dramatically depending on when you prompt them. DeepSeek projected BTC at $500,000–$600,000 in January 2025, and now targets $100,000. That 80% revision in barely a year says more about how these models work than where prices are actually headed. Based on what both AI models project and the catalysts outlined above, here are three scenarios for how XRP and Bitcoin could perform relative to each other through year-end. If the CLARITY Act passes by mid-year and XRP ETF inflows push past $3 billion, XRP could reach $2.50–$4.00 while Bitcoin recovers to $100,000–$120,000. That puts XRP at roughly 80–185% gains versus Bitcoin's 50–80% from current levels. Ripple's banking charter going live and RLUSD adoption scaling across Asia—where Japan already accounts for more than half of Ripple's payment volume — would add fuel. This is the scenario where DeepSeek's aggressive XRP prediction starts looking reasonable. Should the CLARITY Act stall past midterms and ETF inflows slow to $50–$100 million per month, both assets are likely stuck in a range. The BTC price could consolidate between $75,000–$100,000 while the XRP price trades in the $1.50–$2.50 range. Ripple's infrastructure keeps building underneath, but without a regulatory green light, there's no reason for fresh capital to rush in. XRP would still edge Bitcoin on percentage returns since it's climbing from a deeper hole, but the gap stays narrow—closer to what ChatGPT's XRP prediction implies. A wider Iran conflict pushing oil past $90 and a hawkish Fed under Kevin Warsh signaling no cuts in 2026 could send Bitcoin below $60,000—and XRP would take a harder hit. Institutional ETF holders already pulled $6 billion out of BTC funds in early 2026, and another wave of selling could drag XRP toward $0.90–$1.10 while Bitcoin holds $50,000–$60,000. With XRP open interest down 70% and whales sitting on billions in exchange-ready tokens, there's less buying support under the XRP price than at any point since the ETFs launched. Both AI models miss badly here, because neither accounts for what happens when investors sell altcoins first and ask questions later. See for yourself (Sponsor) Several of the largest cryptocurrencies have seen gains while Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) dropped 27.6% over the past year, leading investors to wonder which altcoins could outperform Bitcoin before the end of 2026. Bitcoin is trading around $80,500, 36.2% below its record high of $126,080. It has fallen 4.5% in the last 30 days and 1.3% over the past week. Most major coins have fallen more sharply than Bitcoin in the last week, with only three showing gains: privacy-focused Monero (CRYPTO:XMR) up 7.2%, BNB up 1.4%, and Bitcoin Cash up 0.7%. Ethereum, the second-largest coin, fell by 3.0%. In our analysis, we ranked the top 50 coins based on momentum vs. Bitcoin, potential growth catalysts before the year ends, distance from all-time highs, liquidity, and associated risks. We excluded stablecoins and BNB from this analysis. Five coins stood out as potential candidates, but their success hinges on Bitcoin's future performance. Bitcoin's dominance—its share of the total cryptocurrency market—stands at 59.5%. Altcoins, any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin, usually outperform Bitcoin when this dominance declines. A drop in Bitcoin's market share suggests investors are shifting funds from Bitcoin to other cryptocurrencies. SoFi Active Invest is offering a limited-time promotion. Open an account, fund it with $50 or more, and you could receive up to $1,000 in complimentary stock for Active Invest accounts. See for yourself by clicking here now. (Sponsor) However, that shift hasn't happened. Total cryptocurrency market value fell 4.2% in the 24 hours leading up to today, and trading volume fell 10.8%. The Fear and Greed Index, which measures market sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, read 46, indicating neutral sentiment. Recent fund flows reflect this caution. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $528.4 million on October 21, only to see an outflow of $635.5 million on October 22—the largest one-day outflow since September 24. Spot Ethereum ETFs are looking even weaker, losing $110.5 million on October 22 and cutting total net assets from $17.8 billion on September 25 to $14.6 billion. Ethereum has also dropped 40.3% over the past year, far more than Bitcoin, which is why it did not make our list. Monero is a privacy-focused cryptocurrency that conceals the identities of both senders and recipients. XMR trades around $593, up 7.2% this week, 8.4% over the last month, and 80.2% over the past year. While Monero has shown resilience, it remains 25.7% below its all-time high of $798. However, the liquidity of Monero is a significant concern. XMR's trading volume was only $108.9 million in the 24 hours leading up to today—just a fraction of Bitcoin's $22.1 billion. This thin trading volume means that a few large sell-offs could quickly reverse any gains. Hyperliquid (CRYPTO:HYPE) runs a blockchain designed for decentralized trading. HYPE trades around $75 and is 23.1% below its record of $98. It has gained 90.2% over the past year but has dropped 17.1% in the last month. Another point of concern for Hyperliquid is the supply. Its $16.8 billion market cap is based on just 222.4 million circulating tokens out of a maximum of 1 billion. If all tokens were circulating at the current price, HYPE's market cap would reach roughly $75.4 billion. As those tokens enter circulation, the added supply could weigh on the price even if demand increases. TRON (CRYPTO:TRX) is a blockchain platform for payments and token transfers. TRX trades around $0.33, which is 23.5% below its record high of $0.43. Over the past year, it has gained 6.4%, while Bitcoin has lost 27.6%. TRX's small price swings have protected holders during Bitcoin's downturn. In contrast, NEAR Protocol (CRYPTO:NEAR) has surged 206.3% year to date and trades at about $4.50. However, it saw a 9.5% loss in the 24 hours leading up to October 24 and remains 78.1% below its record high of $20. Quant (CRYPTO:QNT) has skyrocketed 98.8% in the last 30 days to around $178, but it also fell 8.3% in the last week. Both of these coins have outperformed Bitcoin this year, but their rapid gains can vanish just as quickly. First, The Pomp Podcast noted Bitcoin's consolidation between $83,000 and $87,000 in a September 26 episode, but Bitcoin has since slipped below that range. A return above $83,000 would signal a potential Bitcoin recovery. Moreover, spot Bitcoin ETFs need to see more inflow days like the $528.4 million collected on October 21, and Bitcoin dominance should fall below 59.5% for altcoins to thrive. Each potential outperformer also faces its own challenges. Monero could keep beating Bitcoin if it holds gains during downturns. Hyperliquid might surpass Bitcoin if demand pushes HYPE back above $98 while absorbing new token supply. coreStoryFacts.text: Where both AI models disagree is how much stronger.
ChatGPT sees XRP returning roughly 80–150% versus Bitcoin's 65–125%, while DeepSeek projects XRP gaining 260–470% while capping Bitcoin's upside at around 52% from current levels.

ChatGPT and DeepSeek predict XRP outperforms Bitcoin through year-end because XRP's smaller market cap amplifies ETF inflows faster and the CLARITY Act proposes federal commodity classification for XRP.
XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) trades near $1.40 after falling 62% from its July 2025 peak of $3.65.
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) sits around $66,000, down 48% from October's $126,000 high.
The percentage gap between the two models tells the real story.
ChatGPT places XRP in a $2.50–$3.50 base range by late 2026, with a bull case stretching to $5–$10 if ETF inflows accelerate and Ripple's payment corridors scale.

Several of the largest cryptocurrencies have seen gains while Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) dropped 27.6% over the past year, leading investors to wonder which altcoins could outperform Bitcoin before the end of 2026. Bitcoin is trading around $80,500, 36.2% below its record high of $126,080. It has fallen 4.5% in the last 30 days and 1.3% over the past week.

Most major coins have fallen more sharply than Bitcoin in the last week, with only three showing gains: privacy-focused Monero (CRYPTO:XMR) up 7.2%, BNB up 1.4%, and Bitcoin Cash up 0.7%. Ethereum, the second-largest coin, fell by 3.0%.

In our analysis, we ranked the top 50 coins based on momentum vs. Bitcoin, potential growth catalysts before the year ends, distance from all-time highs, liquidity, and associated risks. We excluded stablecoins and BNB from this analysis. Five coins stood out as potential candidates, but their success hinges on Bitcoin’s future performance.

Bitcoin’s dominance —its share of the total cryptocurrency market—stands at 59.5%. Altcoins, any cryptocurrency other than Bitcoin, usually outperform Bitcoin when this dominance declines. A drop in Bitcoin’s market share suggests investors are shifting funds from Bitcoin to other cryptocurrencies.

However, that shift hasn’t happened. Total cryptocurrency market value fell 4.2% in the 24 hours leading up to today, and trading volume fell 10.8%. The Fear and Greed Index, which measures market sentiment on a scale from 0 to 100, read 46, indicating neutral sentiment.

Recent fund flows reflect this caution. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $528.4 million on October 21, only to see an outflow of $635.5 million on October 22—the largest one-day outflow since September 24.

Spot Ethereum ETFs are looking even weaker, losing $110.5 million on October 22 and cutting total net assets from $17.8 billion on September 25 to $14.6 billion. Ethereum has also dropped 40.3% over the past year, far more than Bitcoin, which is why it did not make our list.

Monero is a privacy-focused cryptocurrency that conceals the identities of both senders and recipients. XMR trades around $593, up 7.2% this week, 8.4% over the last month, and 80.2% over the past year. While Monero has shown resilience, it remains 25.7% below its all-time high of $798.

However, the liquidity of Monero is a significant concern. XMR’s trading volume was only $108.9 million in the 24 hours leading up to today—just a fraction of Bitcoin’s $22.1 billion. This thin trading volume means that a few large sell-offs could quickly reverse any gains.

Hyperliquid ( CRYPTO:HYPE ) runs a blockchain designed for decentralized trading. HYPE trades around $75 and is 23.1% below its record of $98 . It has gained 90.2% over the past year but has dropped 17.1% in the last month.

Another point of concern for Hyperliquid is the supply. Its $16.8 billion market cap is based on just 222.4 million circulating tokens out of a maximum of 1 billion. If all tokens were circulating at the current price, HYPE’s market cap would reach roughly $75.4 billion. As those tokens enter circulation, the added supply could weigh on the price even if demand increases.

TRON ( CRYPTO:TRX ) is a blockchain platform for payments and token transfers. TRX trades around $0.33, which is 23.5% below its record high of $0.43. Over the past year, it has gained 6.4%, while Bitcoin has lost 27.6%. TRX’s small price swings have protected holders during Bitcoin’s downturn.

In contrast, NEAR Protocol ( CRYPTO:NEAR ) has surged 206.3% year to date and trades at about $4.50. However, it saw a 9.5% loss in the 24 hours leading up to October 24 and remains 78.1% below its record high of $20.

Quant ( CRYPTO:QNT ) has skyrocketed 98.8% in the last 30 days to around $178, but it also fell 8.3% in the last week. Both of these coins have outperformed Bitcoin this year, but their rapid gains can vanish just as quickly.

First, The Pomp Podcast noted Bitcoin’s consolidation between $83,000 and $87,000 in a September 26 episode, but Bitcoin has since slipped below that range . A return above $83,000 would signal a potential Bitcoin recovery.
Moreover, spot Bitcoin ETFs need to see more inflow days like the $528.4 million collected on October 21, and Bitcoin dominance should fall below 59.5% for altcoins to thrive.

Each potential outperformer also faces its own challenges. Monero could keep beating Bitcoin if it holds gains during downturns. Hyperliquid might surpass Bitcoin if demand pushes HYPE back above $98 while absorbing new token supply. TRON is more likely to outperform if Bitcoin continues to drift downward, as its stable price has offered holders better protection than Bitcoin over the past year.
However, the move into altcoins might not succeed. If outflow trends continue, like the $635.5 million seen on October 22, most altcoins could falter as well.

Looking ahead to the end of 2026, Monero appears to be the top candidate to outperform Bitcoin. Following Monero, Hyperliquid and TRON also show promise. However, in a strong market rally, NEAR and Quant could outshine these three, though their price volatility makes them less reliable choices.

Each of these cryptocurrencies has its own challenges: Monero tends to have lower trading volume, Hyperliquid faces issues with new supply, and TRON may struggle to keep pace as prices rise because of its more stable price movements.

For those invested in altcoins, Bitcoin’s dominance is a crucial metric to monitor. If Bitcoin’s dominance consistently drops below 59.5%, combined with new inflows into spot Bitcoin ETFs, it could signal that investors are starting to shift money into alternative cryptocurrencies.

facts.text: Where both AI models disagree is how much stronger.
ChatGPT sees XRP returning roughly 80–150% versus Bitcoin's 65–125%, while DeepSeek projects XRP gaining 260–470% while capping Bitcoin's upside at around 52% from current levels.

ChatGPT and DeepSeek predict XRP outperforms Bitcoin through year-end because XRP's smaller market cap amplifies ETF inflows faster and the CLARITY Act proposes federal commodity classification for XRP.
XRP (CRYPTO: XRP) trades near $1.40 after falling 62% from its July 2025 peak of $3.65.
Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) sits around $66,000, down 48% from October's $126,000 high.
The percentage gap between the two models tells the real story.
ChatGPT places XRP in a $2.50–$3.50 base range by late 2026, with a bull case stretching to $5–$10 if ETF inflows accelerate and Ripple's payment corridors scale.
From $1.40, that base case implies 80–150% upside.
On the Bitcoin side, ChatGPT projects $110,000–$150,000 as its base, or roughly 65–125% from $66,000.
When asked directly where to put $10,000 between XRP and Bitcoin, ChatGPT picked XRP—citing catalysts that are already active versus Bitcoin still waiting on the Fed.
But the catalysts each model weighs are different.
ChatGPT's XRP price prediction assumes these catalysts keep building without needing a new breakthrough to push prices higher.
DeepSeek takes a much more aggressive stance on XRP.
For Bitcoin, DeepSeek is notably more cautious—its most recent projection targets $100,000 by year-end after a potential drop to $41,000 during Q2 or Q3.

DeepSeek treats XRP's 2026 selloff as temporary noise driven by macro headwinds rather than any weakness in the token's fundamentals, while viewing Bitcoin's recovery as dependent on a reflationary second half.
A wider Iran conflict pushing oil past $90 and a hawkish Fed under Kevin Warsh signaling no cuts in 2026 could send Bitcoin below $60,000—and XRP would take a harder hit.
Institutional ETF holders already pulled $6 billion out of BTC funds in early 2026, and another wave of selling could drag XRP toward $0.90–$1.10 while Bitcoin holds $50,000–$60,000.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
This is the scenario where DeepSeek's aggressive XRP prediction starts looking reasonable.
Ripple's infrastructure keeps building underneath, but without a regulatory green light, there's no reason for fresh capital to rush in.

Anyone can mint the testnet tokens freely for the purpose of testing applications, and thus they have no market value elsewhere. Developers sometimes publish recovery phrases during application testing, but under real conditions on the main network, they wouldn't intentionally be published. passages: 7, Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) co-founder Joseph Lubin said on CNBC that while AI might offer creativity and expertise, it can't create trust, which blockchains like his can help to supply.
In his view, AI and crypto will thus end up merging, becoming the system where programmatic work can be commissioned, completed, and compensated.
The most likely scenario is that Ethereum's capital pulls agents in gradually, with payments flowing through its Layer-2 networks.
There's a little bit of evidence that Lubin's world is already starting to peek into existence.
Here's what it'd mean for Ethereum if that continues.
Today, one of Ethereum's biggest contributions to the AI-in-crypto segment is ERC-8004, a new standard for blockchains that calls for tracking the identities and reputations of AI agents.
Still, there are signs Lubin's vision is taking shape.
Ethereum hosted about 32,343 registered agents as of May 13 of this year, so its count has more than doubled in five months.
That makes Ethereum a practical way to add AI exposure to a well-balanced crypto portfolio , even if agent-driven fees take years to ramp up, which they might.
Monthly agent payments over x402, a standard for paying in stablecoins, peaked at $20.5 million in November 2025, and then fell to $263,863 in September 2026.
Meanwhile, Ethereum collected $17.7 million in transaction fees in the 30 days ending on Oct.
Agents supplied almost none of that, since Ethereum's main chain had settled just 644 agent payments as of Oct.
Watch two numbers: Ethereum's share of registered agents, and monthly x402 payments.

If agents are making payments on Ethereum and doing most of their business there, it'll be bullish for the coin even if the trust element that Lubin is hoping for never becomes as important as he expects.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch. Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups. According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

extraction.body: Complete protection for your devices, online privacy & identity Combines security, performance & privacy features in one app Enhanced protection with device performance booster Did you know that live chat agents on websites can see everything — even messages you never actually sent? This post looks at how this works, and what you can do about it. Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget. It usually appears as a small window in the corner of your screen, complete with an agent’s name and picture. Sometimes these chats simply collect tickets for tech support or sales to process. But often there’s a real person on the other end of the screen. And here’s where many users get an unwelcome surprise: agents can see absolutely everything you type into the chat box, even if you have no intention of sending it. In this article, we break down why this happens and what you can do about it. It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform. Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses. Additionally, real-time chat monitoring enables supervisors to oversee chat interactions, ensuring quality and timeliness.” While that might sound helpful and harmless to some, having their unsent messages watched without their permission can trigger outright panic for others. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send. As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device. Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much . Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how . Another technology that remains largely unknown to the general public is session replay scripts. These tools allow website owners to watch a recording of your visit: how fast you moved your cursor, where you clicked, which pages you browsed, and what you added to your shopping cart. Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong. In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users. On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. If you change your mind about asking a question, edit a sentence, or delete your text entirely, that doesn’t mean no one saw the draft. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews. While you can’t prevent a potential breach on a third-party website, you can — and should — take steps to secure your own browsing session. First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. It’s critical never to share personal data, credit card numbers, logins, passwords, or any other sensitive information with live chat agents. Beyond that, there’s always a risk of landing on a phishing site and entering your account credentials there. To prevent this, we recommend using our security solutions , which block visits to malicious and suspicious websites. We also suggest storing your credentials in Kaspersky Password Manager — our password manager won’t let you auto-fill saved logins and passwords on a fake site. Users of Kaspersky Standard , Kaspersky Plus , and Kaspersky Premium have access to our Private Browsing feature (on Windows and macOS ). It prevents third-party services from tracking your online activity and collecting real-time information about what you do on websites. To minimize the risk of data leaks, keep these tips in mind: Tired of endless digital tracking? Here’s how you can protect yourself and your data: We analyze the first-ever real-world incidents where attackers targeted AI agents deployed in corporate environments. Let’s look at how to use AI as a resume editor without oversharing to build a document that gets past automated screening systems and catches a recruiter’s eye. University students sometimes don’t see the practical value of what they’re studying, and aren’t always sure what to do next. Kaspersky Academy’s free “Cybersecurity. Did you know that live chat agents on websites can see everything — even messages you never actually sent? This post looks at how this works, and what you can do about it.
Virtually every website selling products or services features a live chat widget. It usually appears as a small window in the corner of your screen, complete with an agent’s name and picture.

Sometimes these chats simply collect tickets for tech support or sales to process. But often there’s a real person on the other end of the screen. And here’s where many users get an unwelcome surprise: agents can see absolutely everything you type into the chat box, even if you have no intention of sending it. In this article, we break down why this happens and what you can do about it.

It’s all thanks to a feature known as live typing preview, or real-time typing view, which exists under one name or another in almost every popular customer chat platform. Here’s how the developer of LiveAgent, a customer support system used by more than 40 000 companies, describes it in its blog: “This live chat typing preview allows agents to anticipate questions and deliver faster responses. Additionally, real-time chat monitoring enables supervisors to oversee chat interactions, ensuring quality and timeliness.”

While that might sound helpful and harmless to some, having their unsent messages watched without their permission can trigger outright panic for others. To make matters worse, it’s almost impossible to tell whether the website uses the feature. That is, unless the chat agent admits it to you directly… or replies to a message you decided not to send.

As an alternative, you can run a quick test: type out a message in the chat box, wait 15 seconds, and see if the agent starts typing a response. If they do, you’re almost certainly dealing with real-time typing view. Whether to continue that conversation is up to you. Most importantly, never type personal information into a chat box — even if you are doing so from a Kaspersky Premium device.

Real-time typing view is just the tip of the iceberg. In reality, websites collect far more information than you might think. You’re likely already familiar with cookies, and have probably asked yourself at least once, “Should I accept these or not?” We answer that and other questions in our post Taking the biscuit: why hackers like cookies so much .

Tracking techniques that use web beacons and tracking pixels are not as widely known. To learn why they’re a concern and how to turn them off, check out our post Who is tracking you on the web and how .

Another technology that remains largely unknown to the general public is session replay scripts. These tools allow website owners to watch a recording of your visit: how fast you moved your cursor, where you clicked, which pages you browsed, and what you added to your shopping cart.

Of course, the primary goal of session replay is the same as real-time typing view: improving customer and user experience. It helps companies analyze your behavior, identify friction points, and make improvements. If a customer fails to complete a checkout or encounters a technical issue, developers can review the recording of their session to pinpoint what went wrong.
In theory, it sounds helpful enough: “We will collect a small amount of data about you to make the site better for you.” In practice, however, this approach comes with significant risks for users.

On top of that, users rarely realize an agent can read their message before it’s actually sent. If you change your mind about asking a question, edit a sentence, or delete your text entirely, that doesn’t mean no one saw the draft. Unlike cookies, opting out of this technology is practically impossible. Most chat widgets simply don’t offer a setting to disable typing previews.
While you can’t prevent a potential breach on a third-party website, you can — and should — take steps to secure your own browsing session.

First and foremost, pay close attention to what you type in a chat box. It’s critical never to share personal data, credit card numbers, logins, passwords, or any other sensitive information with live chat agents.

Beyond that, there’s always a risk of landing on a phishing site and entering your account credentials there. To prevent this, we recommend using our security solutions , which block visits to malicious and suspicious websites. We also suggest storing your credentials in Kaspersky Password Manager — our password manager won’t let you auto-fill saved logins and passwords on a fake site.

Users of Kaspersky Standard , Kaspersky Plus , and Kaspersky Premium have access to our Private Browsing feature (on Windows and macOS ). It prevents third-party services from tracking your online activity and collecting real-time information about what you do on websites.

extraction.body: Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month. Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages. It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action. It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month. Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages. Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household. There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram. Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures. Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later. Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images. For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch. Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups. According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls. The biggest differentiator with Tomo ’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos. In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner. Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

BeInCrypto reported Brent crude at $117.42 a barrel on Friday, October 23, its highest level since April. The outlet also said Thursday’s Nasdaq fell 2.6% and the S&P 500 lost 1.2%. The oil-market account identified fresh attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces on Saudi Arabia as the immediate trigger. Saudi Aramco evacuated its headquarters as fighting intensified, while an oil spill near the United Arab Emirates added to concerns about shipping security. BeInCrypto linked the technology-stock selloff partly to concerns about AI spending and described higher energy costs as a potential source of inflation pressure. In its account, persistent inflation could keep Federal Reserve policy restrictive and weigh on speculative assets. A Forbes reference identifies November 10, 2024, as the first time Bitcoin rose above $80,000. The current price level is therefore not a first-ever crossing. A separate May 4, 2026, report carried by TradingView described BTC reaching an intraday high of $80,529, its highest level since January 31. It tied that earlier move to President Donald Trump’s announcement of Project Freedom, an initiative concerning ships stranded around the Strait of Hormuz. Trump announced the operation in a Sunday Truth Social post and called it a “humanitarian gesture” for neutral countries affected by the US -Israeli war with Iran. He said the US would “guide their Ships safely” through the restricted waterways. The operation was scheduled to begin Monday and could involve guided-missile destroyers, more than 100 aircraft and 15,000 service members. Iran denounced the plan as a possible ceasefire violation. Trump warned that interference would “have to be dealt with forcefully.” So the announcement paired a proposed route out for stranded shipping with a continuing risk of confrontation — even as the May market account described traders responding to the prospect of geopolitical relief. extraction.body: Wealthy bitcoin $BTC $84,459.46 holders are increasingly treating their cryptocurrency as an asset to borrow against and generate income from, marking a shift from speculation toward private banking, according to Xapo Bank CEO Seamus Rocca. At the Gibraltar-based bank, customers are seeking cash without selling their bitcoin, putting some of their holdings into income-generating investments, or accumulating more $BTC through interest paid on dollar savings, he said. “Customers are looking for yield and alpha,” Rocca told CoinDesk in an interview, pointing to demand from funds and family offices for accumulation and income products. The behavior reflects bitcoin’s growing maturity, he said. Five or six years ago, the cryptocurrency was primarily viewed as a trading and speculative asset. Today, more holders want financial services built around their existing wealth. Xapo grew out of a bitcoin custody business known for its Swiss bunker storage. Its customers include early adopters who have experienced several halvings (the periodic reductions in new bitcoin issuance), and the rallies and downturns surrounding them. The bank charges an annual membership fee of $1,000, combining dollar banking with access to bitcoin custody, investments and borrowing. Experience has pushed those customers in different directions. Some of the earliest adopters became more willing to take profits as bitcoin reached record prices, having watched gains disappear in previous downturns, Rocca said. Others, including investors who entered around 2018 and 2019, remain determined to hold and prefer borrowing against their coins when they need liquidity. For the profit-takers, selling does not necessarily mean abandoning bitcoin. Some keep the proceeds in dollar savings accounts and receive interest in $BTC , gradually rebuilding their cryptocurrency holdings while retaining cash. Rocca said about 45% of Xapo customers use that feature. Xapo currently advertises a variable base rate of 4.1% on dollar savings, paid in bitcoin, alongside a temporary 4.6% introductory rate for eligible new members. It’s a separate bitcoin credit fund that targets annual returns of up to 4% through lending, exposing investors to credit and counterparty risk. The common thread is the demand to make existing wealth productive. “The theme of this cycle is yield, accumulation, income generation,” Rocca said. Borrowing allows customers to retain exposure to future bitcoin gains, although they also remain exposed to price declines while taking on debt. Traditional banks increasingly acknowledge that clients want bitcoin exposure, Rocca said. Their interest in custody and investment products represents a substantial change from the skepticism he encountered when he began working in crypto in 2016.

It’s a separate bitcoin credit fund that targets annual returns of up to 4% through lending, exposing investors to credit and counterparty risk.
The common thread is the demand to make existing wealth productive.
“The theme of this cycle is yield, accumulation, income generation,” Rocca said.
Borrowing allows customers to retain exposure to future bitcoin gains, although they also remain exposed to price declines while taking on debt.

Traditional banks increasingly acknowledge that clients want bitcoin exposure, Rocca said. Their interest in custody and investment products represents a substantial change from the skepticism he encountered when he began working in crypto in 2016.
“Big banks are slow,” he said, describing institutions where new products require committee approvals and employees are reluctant to champion activities perceived as risky.

Political and regulatory uncertainty adds to that caution. Banks that previously feared repercussions from serving crypto businesses need confidence that a more accommodating environment will endure before committing resources, he said.
For now, some institutions are doing enough to meet customer demand through investment products, while stopping short of services that let clients borrow against or directly manage bitcoin wealth.
“Them being slow is a good opportunity for firms like Xapo Bank,” Rocca said.
He also sees benefits in a measured approach, arguing that another failure involving poorly managed crypto businesses could damage confidence in bitcoin itself.
Rocca expects bitcoin’s next phase of growth to depend on more institutions making long-term allocations.

He argues that some participation through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) has involved arbitrage strategies, which differ from a corporate treasurer deciding to allocate a portion of the company’s assets to bitcoin.
“People called the institutional cycle too early,” he said.
Reduced geopolitical and regulatory uncertainty could help unlock those allocations, potentially pushing bitcoin to $250,000 over the next two to three years, in his view.

Xapo’s customers are less united about the immediate outlook. Some are buying because they believe the market has bottomed out; others are keeping their savings in dollars because they expect further declines, while earning interest in bitcoin.
For Rocca, that mix still points toward accumulation and demand for banking services that help holders build their positions over several years.

passages: That's where Bitcoin works best as a hedge against inflation.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
One 2023 study, bluntly titled "Bitcoin Does Not Hedge Inflation," suggests that Bitcoin tends to fall during inflation scares.
That argues for holding other assets that will hold up against inflation, such as gold, index funds, and real estate, as well as some Bitcoin.

After all, even if it doesn't have the same history as gold, it's easy to see that Bitcoin's value isn't about to be inflated away anytime soon, whether or not it keeps up with gas prices during a major war.
So it's difficult to say that the coin is a good inflation hedge without adding some significant qualifications.
What's more, over the last five years, during which inflation has consistently run well above the Fed's 2% annual target, Bitcoin's price is up 32%.
Gold, the traditional inflation-resistant asset, is up by 129%, and the S&P 500 is up by 69%.
Consumer prices rose 22.8% from September 2021 to September 2026, per the BLS, so Bitcoin did beat inflation across five years.
Bitcoin is often proposed as a way to protect portfolios from inflation.

Bitcoin is mainly a bulwark against currency debasement, the dramatic erosion of a currency's purchasing power, most often caused by governments creating new money faster than the underlying economy grows.
It can succeed against debasement because no matter how much money gets printed, it's simply impossible to print more Bitcoin.
Still, that hedge actually working well is entirely unproven at this juncture.

With U.S. consumer prices up 3.7% through September 2026, many savers want to know whether Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) or gold is the better inflation hedge. This rise exceeds the Federal Reserve’s 2% target . Additionally, the core Consumer Price Index (CPI), which excludes the more volatile food and energy sectors, rose 0.3% in September alone.

Bitcoin is trading around $80,530, which is 36.1% lower than its all-time high. Over the past year, Bitcoin has decreased by 27.4%, and it’s down 4.4% in the last month. However, it has seen a rebound with a gain of 23.4% over the last three months.

Gold has also seen some dips. Tether Gold ( CRYPTO:XAUT ), a token that is backed by physical gold, is trading close to $3,990, down 27.5% from its peak on January 28, and it has decreased by 6.3% in the last month. So, which asset has performed better against inflation, and which one looks more promising as we head into 2027?

In a five-year comparison, gold has significantly outperformed Bitcoin. The price of spot gold increased by 126.1%, rising from $1,780 at the end of October 2021 to $4,024 on October 23, 2026. In contrast, Bitcoin only rose by 28% in the same timeframe, climbing from $62,990 on October 25, 2021.

From December 2021 to September 2026, the consumer price index increased by 19.8%. Both gold and Bitcoin outpaced inflation during this period, but gold performed much better. This trend continues over shorter timeframes as well; since December 2023, gold has gained 95.1%, while consumer prices have climbed just 8.9%.

Over the past decade, Bitcoin has grown nearly 119-fold since its price was $678. While Bitcoin has protected purchasing power over the long term, its monthly fluctuations can be unreliable.

Global central banks are stockpiling gold at an accelerating pace, with some moving reserves out of the U.S. These official buyers generally hold gold for years, providing steady demand on a scale Bitcoin doesn’t have.

Additionally, the money supply continues to expand. As of August 2026, M2, which includes cash, checking deposits, savings, and money market funds, reached a five-year high of $23.3 trillion, up 5.7% year over year—within the normal 5% to 7% range.

Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan argues that Bitcoin’s primary advantage lies in its potential to protect investors from currency debasement, which occurs when increased currency supply reduces buying power. Yet, this value proposition hasn’t translated into a strong performance for Bitcoin in its one-year return.

Recent data suggests gold has been the stronger inflation hedge and appears more stable as we approach 2027. Over the past five years, gold has significantly outpaced inflation and remains a preferred choice, given buying activity from central banks.

While Bitcoin has also been a strong long-term hedge against inflation, it fell 27.4% in a year when prices rose 3.7%. Bitcoin tends to benefit holders who hold it for five years or more , despite sharp declines.

A few key price points could influence this assessment. If Bitcoin rebounds above $87,498, its December 31, 2025, price, it would effectively erase its 2026 losses—a rise of 8.7% from current levels. coreStoryFacts.text: That's where Bitcoin works best as a hedge against inflation.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
One 2023 study, bluntly titled "Bitcoin Does Not Hedge Inflation," suggests that Bitcoin tends to fall during inflation scares.
That argues for holding other assets that will hold up against inflation, such as gold, index funds, and real estate, as well as some Bitcoin.

After all, even if it doesn't have the same history as gold, it's easy to see that Bitcoin's value isn't about to be inflated away anytime soon, whether or not it keeps up with gas prices during a major war.
So it's difficult to say that the coin is a good inflation hedge without adding some significant qualifications.
What's more, over the last five years, during which inflation has consistently run well above the Fed's 2% annual target, Bitcoin's price is up 32%.
Gold, the traditional inflation-resistant asset, is up by 129%, and the S&P 500 is up by 69%.
Consumer prices rose 22.8% from September 2021 to September 2026, per the BLS, so Bitcoin did beat inflation across five years.
Bitcoin is often proposed as a way to protect portfolios from inflation.

Bitcoin is mainly a bulwark against currency debasement, the dramatic erosion of a currency's purchasing power, most often caused by governments creating new money faster than the underlying economy grows.
It can succeed against debasement because no matter how much money gets printed, it's simply impossible to print more Bitcoin.
Still, that hedge actually working well is entirely unproven at this juncture.

One 2023 study, bluntly titled "Bitcoin Does Not Hedge Inflation," suggests that Bitcoin tends to fall during inflation scares.
That argues for holding other assets that will hold up against inflation, such as gold, index funds, and real estate, as well as some Bitcoin.

After all, even if it doesn't have the same history as gold, it's easy to see that Bitcoin's value isn't about to be inflated away anytime soon, whether or not it keeps up with gas prices during a major war.
So it's difficult to say that the coin is a good inflation hedge without adding some significant qualifications.
What's more, over the last five years, during which inflation has consistently run well above the Fed's 2% annual target, Bitcoin's price is up 32%.
Gold, the traditional inflation-resistant asset, is up by 129%, and the S&P 500 is up by 69%.
Consumer prices rose 22.8% from September 2021 to September 2026, per the BLS, so Bitcoin did beat inflation across five years.
Bitcoin is often proposed as a way to protect portfolios from inflation.

Bitcoin is mainly a bulwark against currency debasement, the dramatic erosion of a currency's purchasing power, most often caused by governments creating new money faster than the underlying economy grows.
It can succeed against debasement because no matter how much money gets printed, it's simply impossible to print more Bitcoin.
Still, that hedge actually working well is entirely unproven at this juncture.

With U.S. consumer prices up 3.7% through September 2026, many savers want to know whether Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) or gold is the better inflation hedge. This rise exceeds the Federal Reserve’s 2% target . Additionally, the core Consumer Price Index (CPI), which excludes the more volatile food and energy sectors, rose 0.3% in September alone.
